docs.title: The Science of the Built Environment
docs.text:
Title: The Science of the Built Environment

Target Audience: College undergraduate students at Dunwoody College of Technology in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in construction, architecture, and building-systems programs, including future electrical designers

Prerequisites: None beyond a high-school education. Basic high-school algebra and geometry are helpful.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
This course introduces the properties and applications of common building materials used for foundations, framing, and building systems. It builds a broad understanding of the science of the built environment by showing how materials are selected, combined, and assembled to create buildings that are safe, functional, and durable.

Students examine how concrete, steel, wood, masonry, glass, insulation, and other materials behave under load, moisture, heat, fire, and time. They learn how those behaviors determine the design of structural systems, enclosure systems, and the mechanical, plumbing, and electrical systems that make a building habitable. Along the way, students learn the vocabulary of the construction industry, the sequence of the design and construction process, and the role that each professional, including the electrical designer, plays from concept through commissioning.

The course also treats codes, regulations, and sustainability as design inputs rather than afterthoughts. Students learn to apply building codes, to compare materials by performance, cost, and environmental impact, and to justify material choices with evidence. Because the course is taught in Minneapolis, examples emphasize cold-climate construction: frost-protected foundations, high-performance insulation and air sealing, ice-dam and moisture control, and the Minnesota State Building Code and Minnesota Energy Code. The goal is a technically grounded generalist who can read a set of drawings, talk with specialists, and make sound decisions about how buildings are made.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
• The design and construction process: project phases, delivery methods, and the roles of owner, architect, engineer, contractor, and inspector
  • Construction industry terminology, drawings, and specifications
  • Fundamental physics of buildings: loads, forces, stress and strain, heat, moisture, air, light, and sound
  • Properties of common building materials: strength, stiffness, durability, thermal, moisture, and fire behavior
  • Site work, soils, and foundation systems: shallow and deep foundations, slabs, retaining walls, and frost depth in cold climates
  • Structural systems and framing: wood, steel, concrete, and masonry
  • Building enclosure systems: roofs, walls, windows, air and water barriers, and insulation
  • Building systems: mechanical (HVAC), plumbing, fire protection, and vertical transportation
  • Electrical systems and the role of the electrical designer across design and construction phases
  • Building codes, standards, and regulations: the Minnesota State Building Code, the Minnesota Energy Code, permitting, inspection, fire and life safety, and accessibility
  • Sustainable building materials: embodied carbon, life-cycle assessment, recycled content, and green certification
  • Building durability, maintenance, failure modes, and building forensics

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Detailed structural engineering calculations, such as member sizing and finite element analysis
  • Architectural design theory, aesthetics, and history
  • Construction cost estimating, scheduling, and project finance in depth
  • Detailed electrical circuit design, load calculations, and lighting design beyond an introductory level
  • Civil infrastructure such as bridges, highways, dams, and utilities networks
  • Land development, zoning law, real estate, and urban planning
  • Construction trade skills and hands-on installation techniques
  • Building information modeling (BIM) software operation

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • List the major phases of the design and construction process in order
  • Name the common building materials and state their primary uses in foundations, framing, and enclosures
  • Define common construction industry terms, such as load path, shear wall, header, flashing, vapor barrier, and R-value
  • Identify the main components of a foundation, a structural frame, and a building enclosure
  • Recall the major model building codes and the agencies that adopt and enforce them, including the Minnesota State Building Code
  • Recognize the roles of the owner, architect, engineer, electrical designer, contractor, and building official

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain how dead, live, wind, seismic, and snow loads travel through a structure to the ground
  • Describe how strength, stiffness, ductility, and durability differ among wood, steel, concrete, and masonry
  • Explain how heat, air, and moisture move through a building enclosure and why control layers matter in a cold climate like Minnesota's
  • Summarize how foundations transfer loads to different soil types
  • Explain how a building code is organized and why code requirements exist
  • Describe the contribution of the electrical designer in each phase of design and construction
  • Explain what embodied carbon and life-cycle assessment measure

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Use construction terminology correctly when reading drawings and specifications
  • Apply code tables and provisions to determine requirements such as occupancy classification, egress, and fire-resistance ratings
  • Calculate simple loads, tributary areas, and basic R-values and U-values for a wall assembly
  • Sequence the activities of a small building project from site preparation through occupancy
  • Select an appropriate material for a given structural or enclosure application using stated criteria
  • Interpret a typical wall section and identify each layer and its function

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Analyze a building's structural system to identify its load path, lateral force-resisting system, and critical connections
  • Compare the performance of alternative enclosure assemblies for thermal, moisture, air, and fire control
  • Examine how decisions in one system, such as the structure, constrain choices in other systems, such as mechanical and electrical
  • Diagnose likely causes of common building failures, such as cracking, water intrusion, and condensation
  • Break down the design and construction process to show where information is handed off and where coordination fails
  • Differentiate the properties of materials to explain why each suits one application better than another

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Evaluate a building enclosure for code compliance and expected durability
  • Judge the suitability of a structural system for a given building type, site, and budget
  • Assess alternative materials using performance, cost, constructability, and environmental criteria
  • Evaluate sustainable materials using life-cycle data, certifications, and embodied-carbon values
  • Critique a proposed construction sequence for risks, conflicts, and missing steps
  • Appraise the coordination between electrical design and other disciplines at each project phase

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Develop a materials and systems selection matrix for a small building
  • Design a wall assembly that meets stated thermal, moisture, and fire requirements
  • Prepare a construction sequence and design-phase responsibility chart for a building project
  • Compose a code-compliance checklist for a specific building type
  • Propose a more sustainable alternative for a conventional material or assembly, with supporting evidence
  • Capstone project: Select a small existing or proposed building and produce a complete report that describes its foundation, structural frame, enclosure, and building systems. The report evaluates material choices against code and sustainability criteria, and it recommends improvements.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 21 chapters covering 380 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology - How buildings, materials, and systems are defined and described, including the drawings, specifications, and vocabulary of the construction industry.
  2. The Design and Construction Process - The phases of a project from programming through closeout, the delivery methods, and the roles of the owner, architect, contractor, and subcontractors.
  3. Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings - The forces, stress, strain, heat transfer, and thermal resistance principles that explain how buildings carry loads and resist heat flow.
  4. Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort - How moisture, humidity, pressure differences, and air leakage move through buildings, and how they affect condensation and comfort.
  5. Properties of Building Materials - The mechanical, thermal, moisture, and fire properties that distinguish building materials, and how materials are tested and selected.
  6. Structural Loads and Load Paths - How dead, live, snow, wind, and seismic loads travel through beams, columns, walls, and bracing to the ground.
  7. Wood and Steel Framing - The lumber, engineered wood, and structural steel systems used for framing, along with their connections and typical assemblies.
  8. Concrete and Masonry - The ingredients, mixing, placing, and reinforcing of concrete, and the units, mortar, and grout used in masonry construction.
  9. Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater - How site analysis, excavation, soil properties, groundwater, and frost conditions shape what can be built on a site.
  10. Foundation Systems - The shallow and deep foundations, foundation walls, slabs, and retaining walls that transfer building loads to the soil.
  11. Enclosure Control Layers and Insulation - The water, air, vapor, and thermal control layers of wall assemblies, and the insulation materials that provide thermal control in a cold climate.
  12. Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing - The cladding systems, flashing, windows, doors, and air-sealing methods that complete a wall, plus the interior finishes behind them.
  13. Roof Assemblies - How low-slope and steep-slope roofs shed water, drain, ventilate, and resist ice dams, including green roofs.
  14. HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems - The heating, cooling, ventilation, plumbing, and fire protection systems that make a building habitable and safe.
  15. Electrical Fundamentals and Building Service - Voltage, current, power, and the equipment that brings electricity from the utility into a building.
  16. Electrical Distribution, Lighting, and Design Team Coordination - Wiring, lighting, low-voltage, and renewable systems, and how the electrical designer works with other disciplines through each project phase.
  17. Building Codes, Permits, and Enforcement - How model codes and the Minnesota State Building Code are adopted, applied, and enforced through permits, plan review, and inspection.
  18. Fire Protection and Life Safety Requirements - The code requirements for occupancy, construction type, fire-resistance ratings, egress, and emergency power that protect occupants.
  19. Energy Efficiency and High-Performance Buildings - How energy codes, passive design, and rating systems lead to efficient, high-performance, and net-zero energy buildings.
  20. Sustainable Building Materials - How embodied carbon, life-cycle assessment, and material health are used to compare and select sustainable building materials.
  21. Durability, Maintenance, and Building Failure - What determines a building's service life, how buildings fail from water, movement, and decay, and how they are assessed, renovated, and reused.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
The chapters build from the physics and materials of buildings, through structure, enclosure, and building systems, to codes, sustainability, and durability. Dependencies are respected, so each concept is introduced after the concepts it relies on. Read the chapters in order the first time through.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

Meet Beau, Your Building Guide

Hi, I'm Beau the Beaver, and I like things that are built to last. Here is what I do in this book:

  1. Welcome you at the start of each chapter and tell you why it matters.
  2. Think out loud when an idea changes how you should look at a building.
  3. Tip you off to shortcuts that save time on the job.
  4. Warn you about mistakes that new builders make, and how to avoid them.
  5. Encourage you when a topic is genuinely hard.
  6. Celebrate with you when you finish something real.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's build it right!

docs.title: The Built Environment
docs.text:
The built environment is every human-made space in which people live, work, and move: buildings, the roads and utilities that connect them, and the parks and open spaces shaped around them. It is distinct from the natural environment, although the two constantly exchange energy, water, and materials. Most people in North America spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, so the quality of the built environment is a direct determinant of health, productivity, and safety.

The built environment is best understood as nested scales. At the smallest scale sits a single material, such as a piece of lumber. Materials are assembled into components such as walls, and components combine into buildings. Buildings cluster into neighborhoods, which are linked by infrastructure into cities and regions. A decision at one scale propagates to the others: the insulation chosen for a wall affects the heating load of the building, which in turn affects the demand on the regional electrical grid.

Everything Is a System

Notice that each scale is made of the scale below it. When you can name what a wall is made of and what the wall belongs to, you can trace almost any building problem to its cause.

The table below summarizes the nested scales that we have just described. It adds no new ideas, but it gives you a reference to return to as the book moves between scale levels.

Scale Example Typical concern Material Softwood lumber, concrete Strength, moisture behavior Component Stud wall, window, footing Load, heat flow, water Building A four-story apartment Safety, comfort, energy use Neighborhood A block of mixed-use buildings Access, drainage, shading Region A metropolitan area Utilities, transportation

Worked example: tracing a classroom. Suppose a student is uncomfortable in a college classroom on a January afternoon. At the material scale, the window glass has low resistance to heat flow. At the component scale, the window frame leaks air around its edges. At the building scale, the heating system cannot keep up with the heat loss. At the neighborhood scale, a neighboring tower blocks the low winter sun. Each explanation sits at a different scale, yet all four contribute to one complaint. A builder or designer who thinks only at one scale will miss part of the cause.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
A building is an enclosed, roofed structure intended to shelter people, activities, or goods. This definition separates buildings from other human-made structures such as bridges, towers, and dams, which also carry loads but do not enclose usable interior space. The distinction matters for regulation: building codes address enclosed occupied space, while other structures fall under different standards.

Every building does four jobs at once. It supports itself and its contents against gravity, wind, and snow. It separates the interior from the exterior, controlling heat, air, water, and sound. It serves its occupants with light, power, water, and ventilation. And it protects them from fire and other hazards. Each of these jobs is performed by a different group of components, and conflicts between jobs are the source of most design trade-offs. A large window serves occupants with daylight but weakens the separation job in a Minnesota winter.

Worked example: sorting the jobs. Consider a simple wood-framed house. The studs, joists, and foundation support the building. The siding, sheathing, insulation, and roof separate it from the weather. The furnace, wiring, and plumbing serve the occupants. The smoke alarms and gypsum board protect the occupants. If we remove the insulation, the support and protect jobs are unaffected, but the separate job fails and the serve job (the furnace) must work much harder to compensate.

Job Question it answers Example component Support Will it stand? Footings, studs, beams Separate Will it keep weather out? Roof, wall assembly, windows Serve Can people live and work in it? Heating, plumbing, lighting Protect Will it keep people safe? Fire barriers, sprinklers, exits

docs.title: Building Types
docs.text:
Buildings are grouped by what people do in them, a classification called building types or occupancy. The type controls which code provisions apply, how many exits are required, and how much fire resistance is needed. Four broad categories organize most of the construction industry.

Residential construction covers buildings where people live, from single-family houses to apartment buildings. It is the largest sector by number of projects, and most residential buildings in Minnesota use wood framing because of its cost and speed. Commercial construction covers buildings for business and trade, including offices, shops, restaurants, and hotels, and typically uses steel or concrete frames at larger sizes. Industrial construction covers factories, warehouses, and processing plants, where large open floor areas, heavy floor loads, and process equipment dominate the design. Institutional construction covers schools, hospitals, government buildings, and places of worship, where occupants are often vulnerable or unfamiliar with the building, and life-safety requirements are stricter.

Category Typical examples Design emphasis Residential Houses, apartments Comfort, cost, speed Commercial Offices, retail, hotels Flexibility, appearance Industrial Factories, warehouses Floor loads, large spans Institutional Schools, hospitals Life safety, durability

docs.title: Building Materials
docs.text:
Building materials are the physical substances from which buildings are made. Nearly all of them fall into a few families: wood, steel and other metals, concrete, masonry (brick, block, and stone), glass, plastics and foams, and gypsum products. Each family has a characteristic behavior. Wood is light and easy to work but absorbs moisture. Steel is strong and uniform but loses strength in fire. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension. Masonry resists fire and weather but is heavy. Glass admits light but loses heat easily.

Why not simply choose the strongest material for everything? The answer is that no material is best at every task, and the choice always involves trade-offs among strength, weight, cost, durability, fire behavior, thermal performance, appearance, and environmental impact. Chapter 5 treats these properties in detail. For now, we need only the idea that a material is chosen for a job, and that the same material can be an excellent choice for one job and a poor choice for another.

Beau's Tip: Ask What Job the Material Has

When you meet an unfamiliar material, ask three questions: what load does it carry, what does it keep out, and what happens if it gets wet or hot? Those three answers will tell you most of what you need to know.

Worked example: choosing for the job. A designer needs a foundation wall that will sit against wet soil for decades. Wood would rot, and untreated steel would corrode. Poured concrete resists moisture, carries the soil's load, and is strong in compression, which is the kind of load the wall experiences. A designer needs a floor structure for a small house. Here, dimensional lumber is light, inexpensive, and easy to install. The same designer has chosen concrete for one job and wood for another, and the choices are consistent because each material suits its job.

Material family Strong point Weak point Typical use Wood Light, easy to work Moisture, decay Floor and wall framing Steel High strength Fire, corrosion Frames, connections Concrete Compression, fire Tension, cracking Foundations, slabs Masonry Fire, weather Weight, tension Walls, veneers Glass Light Heat loss Windows

docs.title: Building Systems
docs.text:
A building system is a group of components that work together to perform one function for the whole building. Building systems let us divide a large and complicated building into manageable parts. The six systems we use throughout this book are as follows.

  • Structural system: the frame, foundation, and floors that carry loads to the ground.
  • Enclosure system: the roof, walls, windows, and doors that separate inside from outside.
  • Mechanical system: heating, cooling, and ventilation (often called HVAC).
  • Plumbing system: water supply, drainage, and venting.
  • Electrical system: power distribution, lighting, and low-voltage communications.
  • Fire protection system: sprinklers, alarms, and fire-resistant construction.

The key idea is that the systems are interdependent. The structure must be built before the enclosure can be attached to it. The enclosure determines how large the mechanical system must be, because a leaky enclosure demands more heating. The mechanical and electrical systems need holes through the structure, and the structure cannot be weakened to accommodate them without engineering review. A change in one system therefore ripples into others, which is the reason that designers from every discipline must coordinate (Chapter 16 returns to this topic).

Beau's Thinking: Interdependence Is the Point

Think of the systems like the crew on a job site: any one crew can finish its own work, but the building only works when all of them have fit around each other. That is why we study systems separately in this book and keep returning to how they connect.

Worked example: a leaky wall. Suppose a wall is built with gaps that leak air. The enclosure system now loses heat faster than designed. The mechanical system (a furnace sized for the designed heat loss) cannot keep the rooms warm. The electrical system (a baseboard heater added as a repair) draws more power than the circuit was sized for. A structural problem eventually follows if warm, moist indoor air leaks into the wall cavity and condenses on the framing, which can lead to decay. One construction defect has now touched four systems.

docs.title: Building Science
docs.text: Building science is the applied discipline that explains how buildings behave: how they carry load, move heat and moisture, handle air, and age over time. It draws on physics, materials science, and engineering, and it connects the choices made during design and construction to the performance seen during occupancy. This book follows a building-science approach, which is why the chapters that follow address forces, heat, and moisture before they treat any specific construction system.

docs.title: The Construction Industry
docs.text:
The construction industry is the network of firms and professionals that plan, design, build, and maintain the built environment. It is large: construction typically accounts for several percent of national economic output and employs millions of workers. It is also fragmented, since most firms are small and specialize in one trade or building type. Understanding who does what is useful, because nearly every construction problem is ultimately a question about responsibility and communication.

The main participants are as follows.

  • The owner commissions and pays for the project and sets its goals.
  • The architect leads design and coordinates the design team.
  • Engineers (structural, mechanical, electrical, and civil) design the systems for which they are responsible.
  • The general contractor manages construction, schedules the work, and is responsible for the finished result.
  • Subcontractors are specialist firms, such as electricians, plumbers, and framers, who perform parts of the work.
  • The building official reviews plans and inspects the work for compliance with the code.
  • Suppliers and manufacturers provide materials and products.

Chapter 2 examines how these participants work together through the phases of a project. For now, the key point is that information moves among them through a small set of documents: drawings, specifications, and schedules. Those documents are the subject of the second half of this chapter.

In Minnesota, the industry adapts to a climate with deep frost, heavy snow, and wide temperature swings. These conditions drive many local practices, such as footings placed below the frost depth, high levels of insulation, and a construction season that concentrates exterior work into the warmer months. We will return to these practices throughout the book.

Worked example: following a window. A homeowner (the owner) wants a larger window. The architect draws it, the structural engineer checks that the wall can carry the opening, and the manufacturer supplies the unit. The general contractor orders it, the framing subcontractor builds the opening, and the building official inspects the installation. A single window therefore passes through at least six parties, and the drawings and specifications are what keep them consistent.

Participant Main responsibility Document they mostly produce or use Owner Goals, budget Contract Architect Overall design Drawings, specifications Engineer System design Calculations, drawings General contractor Building the work Schedule, submittals Subcontractor Trade work Shop drawings Building official Code compliance Permits, inspection reports

docs.title: Construction Terminology
docs.text:
Construction terminology is the shared vocabulary that lets professionals describe a building precisely, without ambiguity. A word such as "header" or "flashing" compresses a long description into a single term that every trade understands. Learning the terms is the fastest way to read a drawing, follow a conversation on site, and avoid expensive mistakes, because a misunderstood word on a job site often becomes a wrong part built in the wrong place.

Terms come from several sources. Many are inherited trade words, such as "joist" and "stud." Others are defined by standards and codes, such as "occupancy" and "egress." Still others are specific to a region or a trade, so that the same item may have two names in two places. When you meet a new term, the habit that helps most is to record it with its meaning, the system it belongs to, and a sketch.

Worked example: decoding a sentence. Read this line from a framing note: "Provide a double header over the window opening, bearing on jack studs at each side." A header is a horizontal member that carries loads across an opening. "Double" means two pieces are used together. "Bearing" means the load rests on something. Jack studs are shorter vertical members that support the header. Put together, the note tells the framer to build a two-piece beam above the window that rests on short studs at each side, so that the weight above is carried around the opening rather than through the glass.

Term Meaning System Stud Vertical member in a wall frame Structure Joist Horizontal member supporting a floor Structure Header Member that spans an opening Structure Sheathing Panel covering the frame outside Enclosure Flashing Thin material that directs water out Enclosure Footing Wide base of a foundation Structure Duct Channel that carries air Mechanical Conduit Tube protecting electrical wires Electrical Egress A way out of a building Fire protection

Watch Out: Similar Words, Different Meanings

A common trap is treating "footing" and "foundation" as the same thing, when a footing is only the wide base at the bottom of a foundation. When two terms sound alike, look them up in the glossary before you use them on a drawing or at a job site.

docs.title: Units of Measurement
docs.text:
Units of measurement are the standard quantities used to state sizes, forces, and other properties. Construction in the United States uses two systems. The U.S. customary system measures lengths in feet and inches, and it is used on most drawings and in most trades. The International System (SI, or metric) uses meters and millimeters, and it is the system used in engineering science and in most of the world. Professionals must be fluent in both, because products, standards, and research often arrive in the other system.

Two conventions often confuse beginners. First, lengths on drawings are usually written in feet and inches, such as 12'-6 3/8", where the apostrophe means feet and the quotation mark means inches. Second, engineering calculations usually require decimal feet or decimal inches, so the mixed notation must be converted. Another convention to know is the nominal size of lumber: a "2x4" is labeled with its rough size, but a finished piece actually measures 1.5 in by 3.5 in.

To convert feet-inches to decimal feet, divide the inches by 12 and add the result to the feet:

\[ \text{feet}_{decimal} = \text{feet} + \frac{\text{inches}}{12} \]

Worked example: a mixed-unit length. Convert 12'-6 3/8" to decimal feet. First change the fraction to a decimal: \( 3/8 = 0.375 \), so the inches are \( 6.375 \). Then divide by 12: \( 6.375 / 12 = 0.53125 \). Finally add the feet: \( 12 + 0.53125 = 12.53125 \) ft. To check the answer in metric, multiply by 304.8 mm per foot: \( 12.53125 \times 304.8 \approx 3820 \) mm, or about 3.82 m.

Quantity U.S. customary SI Conversion Length foot (ft), inch (in) meter (m), millimeter (mm) 1 in = 25.4 mm Area square foot (ft²) square meter (m²) 1 m² ≈ 10.76 ft² Force pound-force (lbf) newton (N) 1 lbf ≈ 4.448 N Pressure pounds per square inch (psi) pascal (Pa) 1 psi ≈ 6.895 kPa

Beau's Tip: Always Write the Unit

Write the unit next to every number in your notes and calculations. Measure twice, build once, and a missing unit is the easiest mistake to catch the first time.

docs.title: Scale and Dimensions
docs.text:
A dimension states the size of an object or the distance between two points. A scale is the ratio between a length on a drawing and the real length it represents, which lets a large building fit on a sheet of paper. A scale of 1/4" = 1'-0" means that each quarter inch on the paper represents one foot of the actual building. Floor plans are commonly drawn at this scale, site plans at much smaller ones, and construction details at much larger ones such as 3" = 1'-0".

There are two important rules of practice. First, dimensions govern over scaled measurements: when a drawing states a dimension, use that number rather than measuring the sheet with a ruler, since the paper may have been enlarged or reduced in printing. Second, a drawing should state its scale, and each view on a sheet may have a different scale, so check the label before you measure.

The scale ratio can be calculated directly. If the scale is 1/4" = 1'-0", then 1 in on paper represents \( 1 / 0.25 = 4 \) ft in the building. So the real length \( L \) is

\[ L = \frac{\text{drawn length}}{\text{scale (in per ft)}} \]

Worked example: reading a wall from a plan. A wall measures 6 1/2 in on a plan drawn at 1/4" = 1'-0". The scale is 0.25 in per ft, so \( L = 6.5 / 0.25 = 26 \) ft. If the same wall appeared on a 1/8" = 1'-0" plan, it would measure only \( 26 \times 0.125 = 3.25 \) in. The wall is the same size; only the picture has changed.

Watch Out: Measuring a Printout

A drawing that has been printed at "fit to page" no longer matches its stated scale, which is how people end up ordering materials that are too short. Use the written dimensions, and use a scale ruler only to check a dimension that is missing.

docs.title: Construction Drawings
docs.text:
Construction drawings are the scaled graphic documents that show what is to be built, where, and how. They are the main way a design is communicated from the design team to the builders. A set is organized by discipline, with the architectural drawings first, followed by structural, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical sheets, and each sheet carries a title block listing its number, title, scale, and date. Three principles make a set readable: every sheet is numbered and titled, each discipline uses a letter prefix (A for architectural, S for structural, M for mechanical, P for plumbing, and E for electrical), and the views on each sheet are cross-referenced to other sheets.

Four kinds of views appear in nearly every set, and each is the answer to a different question about the building.

docs.title: Plans
docs.text: A plan is a view from directly above a horizontal cut through a building, normally about four feet above the floor. It shows walls, doors, windows, and room layouts, so it answers the question "what is where?" Floor plans, site plans, framing plans, and roof plans are all plan views.

docs.title: Elevations
docs.text: An elevation is a view of a building face or interior wall seen straight on, without perspective. Elevations show heights, window and door positions, and exterior materials, and so answer "what does it look like, and how tall is it?"

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: A section is a view of an imaginary vertical cut through a building, showing the interior as if the building were sliced open. Sections reveal floor-to-floor heights, foundation depths, and how the layers of the roof and walls fit together.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: A detail is an enlarged view of a small area, such as the connection between a wall and a foundation, at a large scale such as 3" = 1'-0". Details are where the construction of a joint is specified, and many of the building-science failures discussed later in the book occur in poorly drawn or poorly built details.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule is a table that lists repeated items, such as doors, windows, or finishes, with their sizes and properties. A door schedule, for example, lists each door by a mark number, with its width, height, material, and fire rating, so that the drawings can show only the mark and avoid clutter.

View Direction of view Answers the question Plan From above, horizontal cut What is where? Elevation Straight on, from one side How does it look, how tall? Section Vertical cut through the building How is it layered and connected? Detail Enlarged small area How is this joint built? Schedule Table What are the sizes and properties of repeated items?

Worked example: following a window through the set. On the floor plan, a window appears at a wall as a thin symbol with a tag, "W3." On the exterior elevation, the window is shown with its height above the floor. On the window schedule, the tag W3 leads to a row stating that it measures 3'-0" wide by 4'-0" high, double glazed. On a wall section, the same window is shown with its flashing and sill. Four views of the same window each answer a different question, and the tag W3 ties them together.

A quiz mode shows a question such as "Where do you find the thickness of the wall insulation?" and asks the student to click the correct view, with immediate feedback.

Implementation: p5.js with pre-drawn 2D views and a responsive layout.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Specifications are the written technical requirements for materials, products, workmanship, and testing. Where drawings show where and how big, specifications state what quality and by what standard. A typical specification names the product or performance required, the standard it must meet (often an ASTM standard), the installation method, and how the work will be inspected. When the drawings and specifications appear to disagree, the contract documents normally state which governs, so a builder should ask rather than guess.

In the United States, specifications are commonly organized using a standard numbering outline, called MasterFormat, which groups work into numbered divisions such as Division 03 (Concrete), Division 06 (Wood, Plastics, and Composites), and Division 26 (Electrical). The outline lets any trade quickly find the sections that apply to it.

Worked example: drawing versus specification. A drawing shows a concrete slab with the note "4 in slab." The specification, in Division 03, adds that the concrete must reach a compressive strength of 4000 psi at 28 days, contain air entrainment suitable for freeze-thaw exposure, and be cured for seven days. Neither document alone tells the builder everything needed. The drawing gives the geometry, and the specification gives the quality.

docs.title: Symbols and Abbreviations
docs.text:
Symbols and abbreviations are the shorthand used on drawings to save space. A circle with a number may mark a detail callout, a thin line pattern may mean insulation, and letters such as "TYP" (typical), "EQ" (equal), and "GWB" (gypsum wallboard) shorten the text. Each set of drawings includes a symbol legend and an abbreviation list, and a builder should read both before reading the sheets because conventions vary slightly among firms.

You've Laid the Foundation!

You can now describe the built environment as nested scales, name the six building systems, convert feet-inches to decimal feet, and read a plan, elevation, section, and detail. That is a solid foundation to build on, and Chapter 2 shows how a project moves from idea to occupancy.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The built environment is made of nested scales, from a single material to a whole region, and decisions at one scale affect the others.
  • A building supports, separates, serves, and protects, and conflicts among those four jobs drive most design trade-offs.
  • Buildings are classified by use as residential, commercial, industrial, or institutional, and the type determines which code requirements apply.
  • Materials are selected for a job, and no material is best at every job.
  • Six interdependent systems make up a building: structure, enclosure, mechanical, plumbing, electrical, and fire protection.
  • Drawings (plans, elevations, sections, details, and schedules) show where and how big, while specifications state what quality.
  • Dimensions govern over scaled measurements, and every number needs a unit.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The phases of a project from programming through closeout, the delivery methods, and the roles of the owner, architect, contractor, and subcontractors. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapter 1. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 24 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 24 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Design Process 105 Construction Process 65 Project Phases 44 Programming 24 Schematic Design 23 Design Development 22 Construction Documents 21 Bidding and Procurement 16 Construction Administration 10 Design-Bid-Build 5 Commissioning 3 Architect 3 Occupancy and Closeout 2 General Contractor 2 Design-Build 2 Construction Manager at Risk 2 Construction Sequencing 2 Project Owner 1 Subcontractor 1 Integrated Project Delivery 1 Submittals 1 Requests for Information 1 Change Orders 1 Critical Path 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology

From First Idea to Front Door

Every building you will ever work on made the same journey from a client's idea to a set of keys. Once you can see the stages and know who is responsible for each, a busy job site stops looking like chaos and starts looking like a plan. Let's build it right!

Chapter 1 introduced the participants in the construction industry and the documents that carry information among them. This chapter puts those participants in motion. A building is not produced by a single act of design followed by a single act of construction. It emerges from a sequence of phases, each with its own questions, deliverables, and decision-makers, and from a set of contractual arrangements that determine who is responsible when something goes wrong.

To keep the ideas concrete, we follow one invented project from start to finish: the Riverbend Youth Center, a one-story community building in Minneapolis with a multipurpose room, three classrooms, a small kitchen, and offices. Every dollar figure, area, and duration for Riverbend is illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic clear rather than to predict real costs.

docs.title: The Design Process
docs.text:
The design process is the iterative method by which a project team converts an owner's needs into a documented solution that others can price, permit, and build. Its inputs are the owner's goals and budget, the characteristics of the site, and the requirements of the building code. Its outputs are the drawings and specifications introduced in Chapter 1. Between input and output lies a long chain of decisions, and the quality of the building depends on how well those decisions are made and in what order.

Design is iterative because no one can choose the best answer on the first try. The team repeats a four-step cycle: define the problem, generate several candidate solutions, evaluate each against stated criteria, and select and refine one. The cycle then repeats at a finer level of detail. The first pass decides where the building sits on the site, a later pass decides how the roof is framed, and a later one still decides which breaker feeds a particular outlet. Design is also convergent, since each decision removes alternatives and constrains the next. Once the roof is framed in wood, for example, the options for the ceiling, the ductwork, and the lighting shrink accordingly.

Chapter 1 observed that a building supports, separates, serves, and protects, and that these jobs compete. The design process is where those conflicts are resolved on paper before they are resolved in materials. The table below restates the four steps with a Riverbend example for each.

Step Question the team asks Riverbend example Define What must be solved, and what limits apply? The multipurpose room needs daylight without overheating or heat loss Generate What are the plausible options? Large clerestory windows, a few modest windows, or skylights Evaluate How does each option score on the criteria? Daylight, winter heat loss, glare, cost Select and refine Which option do we carry forward, and how do we improve it? Modest south-facing clerestory with shading and high-performance glazing

Worked example: iterating on daylight. The owner wants the multipurpose room to feel bright. The architect first sketches three options and rates each on four criteria. Large clerestory windows score best on daylight but worst on winter heat loss and glare. Skylights score well on daylight but worry the team about leaks and snow. A few modest windows are cheap and tight but leave the room dim. The team selects a narrow south-facing clerestory, then checks it with the mechanical engineer, who reports that the added heat loss is acceptable if the glazing is high-performance. The solution is neither the first idea nor the best on any single criterion. It is the best balance of all four, reached after two passes through the cycle.

Design Is a Funnel

Think of the design process as a funnel: wide and cheap to change at the top, narrow and expensive to change at the bottom. Every phase in this chapter is one more pass through that funnel at a finer level of detail.

docs.title: The Architect
docs.text:
The architect is a licensed design professional who leads the design team and takes primary responsibility for the design of the building. Licensing exists because design errors endanger the public: a state licensing board verifies that the architect has the education, experience, and examination record to be trusted with life-safety decisions. The architect typically holds the design contract with the owner, and the architect's seal on the drawings states that a responsible professional prepared them.

The architect rarely designs everything alone. Structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and civil engineers join the team as consultants, each responsible for the systems in their own discipline, and the architect coordinates their work so that the drawings agree with each other. The electrical designer, who is the focus of later chapters, works within this team, either as part of an electrical engineering firm or as part of a contractor's design-build services. During construction the architect usually continues in a second role as the owner's representative, which we examine under Construction Administration.

docs.title: The Construction Process
docs.text:
The construction process is the coordinated sequence of buying, scheduling, assembling, inspecting, and documenting that turns the construction documents into a physical building. Design is carried out with drawings, and the cost of a mistake is an eraser mark. Construction is carried out with concrete, steel, and lumber, and the cost of a mistake is demolition and rework. This asymmetry explains why the industry invests so heavily in planning before the first shovel enters the ground.

Three flows must be managed simultaneously on every project. Materials must be ordered, delivered, and stored so that they arrive when needed and not before. Labor must be scheduled so that the right trades are on site in the right order. Information must move accurately among owner, designers, and builders, because a trade that works from an outdated drawing builds the wrong thing. The contractor is responsible for coordinating all three flows. The table below lists the main contractor responsibilities that we examine in this chapter.

Responsibility What it means on site Procurement Buying materials and hiring subcontractors, including long-lead items Scheduling Sequencing trades and tracking progress against the plan Coordination Resolving conflicts among trades before work is covered up Safety Protecting workers and the public on the site Quality Building to the documents and passing inspections Documentation Keeping records of submittals, questions, changes, and payments

Worked example: one day on the Riverbend slab. On the morning of the slab pour, the general contractor confirms that concrete trucks are scheduled for 7:00. The reinforcing steel has been placed, and the building inspector has approved it the afternoon before. The electrical subcontractor's underground conduit is in place, and the plumbing subcontractor's underground pipes have been tested and inspected. Once the concrete covers those pipes and conduits, a missing sleeve means saw-cutting the slab. The contractor therefore walks the site with each trade before the first truck arrives. A pour that appears to be a single task is actually the end point of five trades' work, and the contractor's real job is to make sure all of them have finished before it starts.

docs.title: The General Contractor
docs.text: The general contractor (GC) is the firm that holds the prime contract with the owner to construct the project and is responsible for all of the work, including work done by others. The GC provides a project manager, who handles the paperwork and money, and a superintendent, who runs the site day to day. The GC decides means and methods, meaning how the work is carried out and in what order, because the construction documents describe the finished result and not the process of getting there. This responsibility is why the architect, who observes the work, does not supervise it.

docs.title: The Subcontractor
docs.text: A subcontractor is a specialty firm hired by the general contractor to perform a portion of the work, such as concrete, framing, roofing, plumbing, mechanical, or electrical. On most commercial buildings, subcontractors perform the majority of the physical work, and the GC acts as the manager who coordinates them. A subcontractor has a contract with the GC and none with the owner, so questions and payments flow through the GC. Some trades are regulated; in Minnesota, for example, electrical work is performed by electricians and electrical contractors licensed through the state. Large subcontractors may hire their own sub-tier firms, and the general contractor remains responsible for the entire chain.

docs.title: Project Phases
docs.text:
Project phases are the standard stages through which a building project moves from first idea to occupied building. Each phase answers a different question, produces defined deliverables, and ends with the owner's approval before the next phase begins. The approval, often called a phase gate, protects the owner and the team from building on decisions that have not been confirmed.

The eight phases used in this chapter are programming, schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding and procurement, construction (with construction administration), commissioning, and occupancy and closeout. The first four are the design phases, in which the building exists only on paper. The last four are the construction and delivery phases, in which the building takes physical form and is handed over. The following sections define each phase in turn, so the table below is best read as a map to return to rather than a lesson on its own.

Phase Main question Principal deliverable Electrical designer's contribution Programming What does the owner need? Written program, budget Identify special power needs Schematic design What overall form works? Site plan, floor plans Estimate service size Design development How will it be built? Refined plans, system selections Locate panels, lay out lighting Construction documents Exactly what is to be built? Drawings, specifications Produce E-series sheets and Division 26 specifications Bidding and procurement Who will build it, and for how much? Signed construction contract Answer bidder questions Construction Is it built as designed? Completed work Review submittals, answer questions Commissioning Does it work as intended? Test reports Verify controls and lighting Occupancy and closeout Is it ready to use? Certificate of occupancy, records Deliver record drawings

The reason for the phase structure is the relationship between decisions and the cost of changing them. Early in a project, the team can still influence nearly everything about the building, and changes cost almost nothing because they are lines on paper. As the project proceeds, the team's influence falls while the cost of changing course rises, since each decision is built on by the next and finally embodied in physical work.

Worked example: moving one wall. Suppose the owner of Riverbend asks to enlarge a classroom by moving a wall four feet. During schematic design, the architect moves a line on one floor plan, which takes an hour. During construction documents, the change must be coordinated across the architectural, structural, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical sheets, and may take several days of work by several people. After the wall has been framed and the electrical conduit installed, the change means demolishing finished work, re-routing wiring, revising the drawings, and issuing a change order, a process that could take weeks and a considerable sum. The wall is the same four feet in every case. Only the phase differs.

Two lines are drawn: "Ability to influence the design" (falling from left to right) and "Cost of making a change" (rising from left to right). docs.title: The Project Owner
docs.text:
The project owner is the person or organization that commissions the project, pays for it, and has the authority to make final decisions about its goals, budget, and schedule. Owners may be private companies, nonprofit organizations, government agencies, or individuals. Public owners are usually bound by procurement laws that require competitive bidding, while private owners have more freedom to choose how they select a builder.

The owner sets the direction at the start and approves each phase gate along the way. The most common source of delay and expense on projects is slow or reversed owner decisions, which is why a team should identify at the outset a single person with authority to speak for the owner. For Riverbend, the owner is a nonprofit organization, and its executive director holds that role. Experienced owners also write down the performance they expect from the building, in a document often called the owner's project requirements, which the commissioning process later uses as the test of success.

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
Programming is the first design phase, in which the team documents what the building must do before anyone draws what it looks like. The result is the program, a written statement of the spaces required, their sizes, how they relate to each other, the performance expected of each, the budget, and the schedule. The architect gathers this information through interviews with the people who will use the building, visits to similar facilities, and analysis of the site.

A program is useful only if it can be checked, so it is expressed in numbers. Each space gets an area, and the areas are added to give the net area, which is the usable floor space inside rooms. A building also needs corridors, walls, mechanical rooms, and shafts, which are not part of any room. The ratio of net area to the total building area is the efficiency, and the gross area follows from it:

\[ \text{gross area} = \frac{\text{net area}}{\text{efficiency}} \]

Worked example: sizing Riverbend. The owner lists the spaces below. The net area totals 6,300 ft². Assume an efficiency of 0.70, a plausible value for a building of this type, so the gross area is \( 6{,}300 / 0.70 = 9{,}000 \) ft². With an illustrative budget of $4.5 million, the target is \( 4{,}500{,}000 / 9{,}000 = \$500 \) per gross square foot. If similar buildings in the region have been costing more than that, the team learns it now, while the cure is to trim the program or raise the budget, rather than after the drawings are finished.

Space Count Area each (ft²) Total (ft²) Multipurpose room 1 2,400 2,400 Classrooms 3 600 1,800 Kitchen 1 500 500 Offices 3 120 360 Storage 1 340 340 Lobby and restrooms 1 900 900 Net total 6,300

The electrical designer contributes at this stage by asking what equipment the spaces will contain. A commercial kitchen, a stage lighting system, or planned electric vehicle charging all affect the size of the electrical service, and each is far easier to include now than to add later.

docs.title: Schematic Design
docs.text:
Schematic design is the phase in which the architect explores the overall form of the building: where it sits on the site, its shape and height, and how the rooms are arranged. The deliverables are a site plan, preliminary floor plans, rough elevations or a simple massing model, a short description of the proposed structure and building systems, and a preliminary cost estimate. The drawings are sketchy by intention, since the purpose is to compare ideas and not to specify materials.

Good schematic design presents the owner with a small number of genuinely different options and the evidence to choose among them. The shape of the building matters because the exterior surface, which includes walls, roof, and floor, is where heat escapes, water enters, and costs accumulate. A long, thin building has more exterior wall for the same floor area than a compact one, but it may also have better daylight and simpler structure.

Worked example: three options for Riverbend. The architect develops three schemes and brings them to the owner with a comparison.

Option Description Strengths Concerns A One-story rectangular bar, 120 ft by 75 ft Simplest structure, easy accessibility, lowest cost Large roof and foundation, less daylight in the center B L-shaped one-story building around a south-facing courtyard Daylight, outdoor space for programs More exterior wall, higher cost C Compact two-story block Smaller roof and footprint, saves site area Needs an elevator and stairs, adds cost and complexity

The owner, balancing the budget against the wish for outdoor space, chooses a hybrid of A and B: a one-story bar with a small south-facing entry court. At the end of the phase, the owner signs off on the plan, and the team agrees not to revisit the basic layout without a formal decision. The electrical designer uses the approved scheme to estimate the building's electrical demand and to contact the electric utility about the service connection, since a utility may need months to deliver a transformer.

docs.title: Design Development
docs.text:
Design development is the phase in which the team takes the approved schematic design and decides how it will actually be built. Structure, enclosure, mechanical, plumbing, electrical, and fire-protection systems are chosen and sized, materials and assemblies are selected, dimensions are fixed, and equipment locations are coordinated. The deliverables are larger-scale plans, sections, and elevations, outline specifications naming the principal materials and products, and an updated cost estimate.

Design development is where the building's science is largely settled. The choices made here, such as the type of roof structure, the insulation in the walls, or the kind of heating system, determine how the building will carry loads and manage heat, air, and moisture for decades. The end of the phase is sometimes called a design freeze: after the owner approves, changes become costly because the next phase will turn every decision into detailed drawings.

Worked example: a long-span room at Riverbend. The multipurpose room needs a 40 ft clear span with no columns. The structural engineer compares glued-laminated wood beams, steel joists, and wood trusses for cost, weight, and fire behavior, and the team selects glued-laminated beams. The mechanical engineer decides to place the rooftop heating-and-cooling unit near the kitchen, so that the ducts stay short, and checks that the roof can carry its weight. The electrical designer puts the main switchboard in a room adjacent to the kitchen and lays out the gym lighting. The updated estimate arrives at $4.77 million, which is 6 percent over the $4.5 million budget. The team now performs value engineering, a systematic search for savings that keep the required performance, and trades expensive floor finishes in the classrooms for durable ones that cost less. The structure, the enclosure, and the systems stay as designed.

docs.title: Construction Documents
docs.text:
Construction documents are the final drawings and specifications that define the work in enough detail for contractors to price it, for the building official to review it for a permit, and for tradespeople to build it. They are the legal core of the construction contract. The drawings are organized by discipline, using the sheet prefixes introduced in Chapter 1 (A, S, M, P, and E), and the written specifications are organized by division. Together with the conditions of the contract and the bidding forms, they make up a bound set often called the project manual.

Three audiences read the documents, and each has a different need. Bidders need quantities and quality standards to set a price. The building official needs evidence that the design meets the code, and Chapter 17 treats the permit and plan-review process in detail. The builders need unambiguous instructions. A gap or a conflict in the documents does not disappear; it turns up during construction as a question, a delay, or a change order.

For this reason the team conducts a coordination review before the documents are released, in which the drawings from each discipline are overlaid to look for conflicts. Coordination is among the most valuable work done in the phase.

Worked example: a clash found on paper. During the coordination review, the engineer notes that a 24 in deep supply duct on the mechanical drawings passes through the same space as a glued-laminated beam on the structural drawings. On site, this discovery would stop the framers, trigger a question to the design team, and probably require a change order. On paper, it costs a revised sheet and a half-hour of coordination: the duct is shifted six inches and routed beneath the beam. A set for a building the size of Riverbend might contain on the order of 60 sheets and several hundred pages of specifications, so a systematic review is the only way to find such conflicts reliably.

docs.title: Bidding and Procurement
docs.text:
Bidding and procurement is the phase in which the owner selects the builder and secures the materials, equipment, and subcontracted trades needed for the project. Bidding is a structured competition in which contractors submit prices for the work described in the documents. Procurement is the broader task of buying, and it includes ordering long-lead items, which are products such as switchgear, elevators, or custom windows that take months to manufacture and can control the schedule.

The usual bidding sequence is as follows.

  1. The owner advertises the project or invites selected contractors to bid.
  2. Contractors review the documents, and may attend a pre-bid conference to ask questions.
  3. The architect issues addenda, which are written changes or clarifications to the documents during bidding.
  4. Bidders submit sealed bids on a specified date, and the bids are opened and recorded in a bid tabulation.
  5. The owner evaluates the bids, and awards the contract to the lowest bidder who is both responsive (the bid follows the instructions) and responsible (the firm has the capability and record to finish the job).

Many bid forms also include alternates, which are priced options the owner may add to or subtract from the base bid, depending on what the budget allows. Public owners are generally required by law to advertise their projects and to award them to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder.

Worked example: bids for Riverbend. Three general contractors bid. Alternate 1 adds an upgraded exterior wall finish to the entry court. The owner decides after the bids are opened whether to accept the alternate.

Bidder Base bid Alternate 1 Base plus Alternate 1 Contractor A $4,380,000 +$90,000 $4,470,000 Contractor B $4,400,000 +$30,000 $4,430,000 Contractor C $4,520,000 +$50,000 $4,570,000

Without the alternate, Contractor A has the lowest price. With it, Contractor B does, because B's price for the extra work is lower. Public owners therefore state in advance how alternates will be used to determine the low bidder, so that the result does not depend on the order in which bids are opened. Riverbend accepts the alternate, awards the contract to Contractor B at $4,430,000, and the project moves into construction.

docs.title: Project Delivery Methods
docs.text:
Bidding is only one of several ways to organize a project. A delivery method is the contractual arrangement that determines who is under contract with the owner, when the builder joins the team, and how the price is set. Each method allocates risk, speed, and control differently. The four methods covered here run from the traditional and sequential to the highly collaborative.

Four Acronyms Is a Lot

Delivery methods blur together for most students on a first reading, so that is normal. You already know how to sort by responsibility, so ask two questions of each method: who is the owner under contract with, and when does the builder join the team? Try filling in the comparison table at the end of this section from memory, then check it against the text.

docs.title: Design-Bid-Build
docs.text:
Design-bid-build (DBB) is the traditional method, in which the three activities happen in strict sequence. The owner first hires an architect, who completes the design. The owner then bids the finished documents to contractors and awards a construction contract to the low bidder. The builder joins the project only after the design is done. The owner has two separate contracts, one with the architect and one with the general contractor, and the two firms have no contract with each other.

The method's strength is its clarity and its competitive price: every bidder prices the same complete documents, and the owner knows the cost before construction starts. Its weaknesses follow from the same sequence. The builder's knowledge of costs and methods is not available during design, the schedule is long because nothing is built until the design is finished and bid, and the architect and contractor may disagree when problems arise.

Worked example: Riverbend as design-bid-build. Riverbend was bid in the Bidding and Procurement section above, so it is a DBB project. Its timeline runs 10 months for design, 1 month for bidding, and 10 months for construction, for a total of 21 months from the start of design to completion. The owner gets a firm price of $4,430,000 before construction begins, and the team uses the documents as the standard when disputes arise.

docs.title: Design-Build
docs.text: Design-build (DB) is a delivery method in which the owner signs a single contract with one entity, usually a contractor, who is responsible for both design and construction. The architect and engineers work as part of the design-build team. The method gives the owner a single point of responsibility and allows construction to begin on early work, such as the foundation, while the rest of the design is still being completed. These overlaps often shorten the schedule, and Riverbend might finish in about 17 rather than 21 months under this method, an illustrative saving. The trade-off is that the owner has less independent oversight of the design, and the price is set earlier, when less is known.

docs.title: Construction Manager at Risk
docs.text: Construction manager at risk (CMAR) is a method in which the owner hires a construction manager during design, as an adviser, and then the same firm agrees to build the project for a guaranteed maximum price (GMP), which is a ceiling price that the construction manager must not exceed. The owner holds separate contracts with the architect and the construction manager, so the design stays independent. The builder contributes cost and schedule advice early, which helps the team stay within budget, and the construction manager bears the risk of overruns above the guaranteed price. The firm is chosen on qualifications and fee rather than lowest price alone.

docs.title: Integrated Project Delivery
docs.text:
Integrated project delivery (IPD) is a collaborative method in which the owner, architect, contractor, and key subcontractors sign a single multi-party agreement and share both risk and reward according to the project's results. Key trades such as electrical and mechanical join the team at the start, and decisions are made jointly. The aim is to move decisions earlier, which, as the cost-of-change curve showed, is when they are cheapest. IPD demands trust and early commitment from every party, and it is less common than the other methods. It extends CMAR by bringing the designers and builders under one set of shared incentives rather than separate contracts.

The table below summarizes the four methods that the preceding sections defined.

Method Owner's contracts Builder joins Price basis Typical strength Design-bid-build Architect and contractor, separately After design is complete Lowest bid Price clarity, competition Design-build One design-builder At the start Negotiated lump sum Speed, single responsibility CMAR Architect and construction manager, separately During design Guaranteed maximum price Early cost advice Integrated project delivery One multi-party agreement At the start, with key trades Shared target cost Collaboration, early decisions

docs.title: Construction Administration
docs.text:
Construction administration (CA) is the set of services that the architect and engineers perform during construction to confirm that the work conforms to the construction documents and to administer the contract between owner and contractor. It includes periodic site visits, review of submittals, answers to questions from the contractor, evaluation of proposed changes, review of the contractor's applications for payment, and a determination of when the work is substantially complete.

CA has a built-in limit that students often miss: the design team observes the work but does not direct it. The contractor remains responsible for means and methods, for the schedule, and for safety on the site. The architect's visits are periodic, and their purpose is to protect the owner by checking that what is being built is consistent with what was designed, not to inspect every detail.

Money is one of the most routine CA tasks. Each month the contractor submits an application for payment, which lists the percent of each part of the work completed. The owner usually withholds retainage, a percentage of each payment (commonly 5 to 10 percent, set by the contract) that is held back until the work is complete, as an incentive to finish and correct defects. The architect reviews the application, visits the site to check that it is accurate, and certifies the amount due.

Worked example: a Riverbend payment application. The contract is for $4,430,000, retainage is 5 percent, and previous payments total $600,000. By the end of the fourth month, the architect agrees with the contractor that 30 percent of the work is in place:

\[ \text{earned to date} = 0.30 \times 4{,}430{,}000 = \$1{,}329{,}000 \] \[ \text{payment due} = 1{,}329{,}000 - (0.05 \times 1{,}329{,}000) - 600{,}000 = \$662{,}550 \]

The retainage withheld to date is $66,450. The contractor does not receive that amount until the work is complete.

Three kinds of paperwork carry most of the information between the contractor and the design team during construction. We define each in turn and then look at how they travel.

docs.title: Submittals
docs.text: Submittals are documents, such as shop drawings, product data sheets, and physical samples, that the contractor sends to the design team for review before ordering or installing certain products. Their purpose is to confirm that the contractor has understood the design and that the proposed product satisfies the specification. A subcontractor prepares the submittal, the general contractor checks it, and the architect or engineer returns it with a status such as approved, approved as noted, revise and resubmit, or rejected. For example, the electrical subcontractor submits the manufacturer's data and dimensions for the main switchboard, and the electrical engineer checks that its ratings and size match the design before it is ordered.

docs.title: Requests for Information
docs.text:
A request for information (RFI) is a written question from the contractor to the design team, asking for clarification when the documents are unclear, incomplete, or in conflict. The design team answers in writing, and the answer may become a change to the documents. RFIs create a record, which protects both sides: the question, the date, and the answer are on file if a dispute later arises about what was intended.

Beau's Tip: Send the Answer With the Question

Before you send an RFI, cite the sheet and detail number, state the conflict in one sentence, and propose how you would resolve it. A question that arrives with a suggested answer usually comes back faster, because the designer can simply say yes or no.

docs.title: Change Orders
docs.text:
A change order is a written modification to the construction contract that adjusts the scope of work, the contract price, the contract time, or any combination of the three, and is signed by the owner, the architect, and the contractor. Changes arise for three common reasons: the owner wants something different, the site holds a surprise such as poor soil, or the documents contain an error or omission. Some change is normal, but a project with many changes is often a project with weak documents or late owner decisions.

Worked example: soft soil at Riverbend. While excavating for the footings, the crew finds a pocket of unsuitable fill beneath the kitchen wing. The contractor submits an RFI, and the geotechnical engineer prescribes the removal of the fill and its replacement with compacted gravel. The contractor prices the work at $38,000 and four additional days, and the three parties sign a change order. The contract sum rises to $4,468,000, and the contract time grows by four days.

Watch Out: The Verbal Go-Ahead

A common trap is starting extra work on a verbal go-ahead from someone at the site, because the change looks small and the schedule is tight. The risk is that no one has agreed on the price, so a dispute later may leave the contractor unpaid. Wait for the signed change order or a written directive, even for small changes.

The paths that RFIs, submittals, and change orders take among the project participants are worth studying together, because the same few channels carry them all.

Subcontractor prepares shop drawings. 2. General contractor checks and forwards. 3. Architect and engineer review. 4. Returned to the general contractor, who returns it to the subcontractor." Hovering over an edge shows whether it is a contract or an informal communication path.

docs.title: Construction Sequencing
docs.text:
Construction sequencing is the planning of the order in which the activities of a project are carried out. The order is not arbitrary. Some activities must follow others for physical reasons, since walls cannot be framed before the floor exists. Other activities are ordered to protect work already done, to allow inspections before work is covered, or to avoid trades blocking each other. A typical wood-framed building follows this general order: site preparation and excavation; footings and foundation walls; underground utilities; slab and floor structure; wall and roof framing; roof covering and windows, which make the building dried in or weather-tight; rough-in of mechanical, plumbing, and electrical systems; insulation and wall finishes; interior finishes; and final testing.

In Minnesota, the calendar shapes the sequence. The contractor tries to complete the foundation and the dry-in before hard winter, so that interior work can proceed in heated, protected space. A project that cannot be dried in before freezing weather faces temporary heat, cold-weather concrete practices, and delays, all of which increase cost.

docs.title: The Critical Path
docs.text:
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities from the start of the project to its finish, and it determines the shortest possible duration of the project. A delay in any critical activity delays the whole project. Other activities have float, meaning the amount of time they can slip without delaying completion. Planners find the critical path by calculating each activity's earliest start and earliest finish from its duration and the activities that must precede it.

Worked example: the Riverbend structure. Consider the following eight activities, with durations in working days.

Activity Duration Must follow Earliest start Earliest finish Float A. Excavate 4 None 0 4 0 B. Pour footings 3 A 4 7 0 C. Foundation walls 5 B 7 12 0 D. Underground utilities 4 C 12 16 0 E. Pour slab 2 D 16 18 0 F. Order roof trusses 15 None 0 15 9 G. Frame walls 6 E 18 24 0 H. Set trusses 3 G and F 24 27 0

The activity H cannot start until both G and F are finished, so it starts at day 24, the later of day 24 and day 15. The critical path is A, B, C, D, E, G, H, a total of 27 days. The truss order has 9 days of float, so a delivery delay of up to 9 days has no effect on completion. A delay of 10 days would push H's start to day 25, and the order would become critical. This is why a planner watches long-lead procurement carefully.
