docs.title: Electrical Plans
docs.text:
Electrical plans are the scaled drawings, usually on sheets numbered with the prefix E, that show where electrical equipment and devices are located and how they are connected. A typical set includes a site plan showing the service and exterior lighting, power plans showing receptacles and equipment connections, lighting plans showing fixtures and switches, the one-line diagram, panel schedules, and detail sheets. A legend explains each symbol and an abbreviation list defines the notes.

The plans follow common reading conventions. A receptacle is a small symbol on a wall. A line with arrowheads that extends from a device toward a panel is a home run, which carries the circuit to its panelboard. A label next to a device such as "LP-1-7" means panel LP-1, circuit 7, so the electrician can find the breaker. The plans work only when they agree with the architectural, structural, and mechanical sheets, which is why coordination meetings are held before they are released.

Beau's Tip: Read the Home Runs

To check any outlet on a plan, find its circuit label, such as LP-1-7, and then look up circuit 7 on panel LP-1's schedule. If the load on the schedule does not match the room, you have found an error on paper before it becomes an error in the wall.

docs.title: Conductors
docs.text:
A conductor is a wire or cable, made of a metal that carries current easily, that serves as the path for electricity in a circuit. Building conductors are almost always copper or aluminum. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper but has higher resistance for a given size, so it is common in large feeders, where the savings are significant. Wire sizes follow the American Wire Gauge for small sizes and a kcmil (thousand circular mils) scale for the largest, and the insulation is rated for temperature and moisture. A common insulation designation is THHN/THWN-2, a thermoplastic that works in dry and wet locations.

The size of a conductor is set by several checks, which Chapter 15 introduced. It must be large enough that its ampacity exceeds the load current after any code adjustments, and the voltage drop must stay acceptable. Ampacity is reduced when many conductors share a conduit or when the ambient temperature is high. Conductor colors follow convention. Neutrals are white or gray, equipment grounds are green or bare, and the phase conductors in a 208 V system are conventionally black, red, and blue, while 480 V systems conventionally use brown, orange, and yellow.

docs.title: Conduit
docs.text:
Conduit is a tube, usually metal or plastic, that protects conductors from damage and routes them through a building. Common types are EMT (electrical metallic tubing, a thin-wall steel tube used indoors), rigid metal conduit for harsher conditions, PVC for underground and wet locations, and flexible metal conduit for the final connection to vibrating equipment. Where many circuits travel together, a cable tray, an open metal ladder or trough, is used instead of individual conduits.

Codes limit how much a conduit can hold, so that wires have room to be pulled in and can shed heat. In most cases, the conductors may fill no more than about 40 percent of the conduit's cross-section, which means a half-inch EMT commonly holds about nine 12 AWG conductors. Conduit also limits how much it can bend between pull points, commonly four quarter bends. Underground conduit is buried deep enough to avoid damage from digging, commonly 18 to 24 inches, and it must be sealed where it enters a building, because a cold-climate conduit can carry moist outdoor air or groundwater into a warm electrical room. The designer must therefore coordinate the routes with the foundation and enclosure systems of earlier chapters.

docs.title: Grounding and Bonding
docs.text:
Grounding is the connection of an electrical system to the earth, and bonding is the connection of all the metal parts of the system to one another. The two work together but do different jobs. Grounding limits the voltage that lightning or utility surges can place on the system and holds the system near earth potential. Bonding makes all exposed metal, such as enclosures, conduits, and equipment frames, electrically continuous, so that a fault finds a low-resistance path back to the source.

The building's grounding electrode system connects the electrical system to the earth through ground rods, buried metal water pipe, and, where available, the steel reinforcement in a concrete footing, called a concrete-encased electrode. The footings and foundations of Chapter 10 therefore play an electrical role, so the electrical designer must coordinate with the structural engineer and the contractor before the concrete is poured. At the service entrance, a main bonding jumper ties the neutral to the ground, and this connection occurs only there.

Worked example: why bonding makes the breaker trip. Suppose a hot wire loosens and touches a metal equipment enclosure. If the enclosure is bonded with a good equipment grounding conductor, with a total resistance of about 0.5 ohm, the fault current is \( 120/0.5 = 240 \) A. A 20 A breaker trips almost instantly on that surge, and the enclosure is de-energized. If the enclosure were connected only to a ground rod with 25 ohms of resistance, the current would be only \( 120/25 = 4.8 \) A, far below the breaker's trip point, so the enclosure would stay energized at a dangerous voltage. Bonding, not the earth connection, is what trips the breaker.

docs.title: Receptacles
docs.text:
A receptacle is a socket in a wall, floor, or ceiling into which a plug connects to deliver power to a portable device, commonly called an outlet. The ordinary general-purpose receptacle is rated 15 or 20 A at 120 V, and a 20 A receptacle has a T-shaped slot that accepts either plug. Codes require special types in certain places. GFCI receptacles, which trip when a few milliamperes leak to ground, are commonly required near water, such as kitchens, restrooms, and outdoors. Tamper-resistant receptacles, which have shutters that block objects other than plugs, are commonly required in schools and child care facilities such as Riverbend's classrooms. Outdoor receptacles must be weather-resistant and have covers that protect them even while a cord is plugged in.

The designer chooses the type, the number, the circuit, and the mounting height. Accessibility guidelines commonly place receptacles between 15 and 48 inches above the floor so that people using wheelchairs can reach them (Chapter 17).

docs.title: Lighting Systems
docs.text:
A lighting system is the combination of luminaires (complete light fixtures), lamps or light-emitting diode (LED) modules, drivers, controls, and wiring that provides light for seeing and working. Today almost all new lighting uses LEDs, which produce more light per watt than older sources and last far longer. Lighting design is measured in a few standard quantities. A lumen is a measure of the total light a source emits, and a footcandle is one lumen falling on one square foot. Efficacy is lumens per watt, and color temperature in kelvins describes whether a light looks warm (about 2,700 K) or cool (about 5,000 K). Energy codes also limit the lighting power density, the watts of lighting per square foot (Chapter 19).

Worked example: the lumen method for a classroom. The lumen method estimates how many luminaires a room needs. Suppose a 600 ft² Riverbend classroom needs an average of 40 footcandles at the desks (an illustrative target). The light that must reach the work surface is \( 40 \times 600 = 24{,}000 \) lumens. Not all the light a fixture emits reaches the desks, since some is absorbed by walls and ceilings, and light output falls as fixtures age and dust collects. A coefficient of utilization of 0.70 and a light loss factor of 0.80, both illustrative, account for those effects, so the fixtures must emit \( 24{,}000/(0.70 \times 0.80) \approx 42{,}900 \) lumens. A luminaire that emits 4,000 lumens would be needed in a quantity of \( 42{,}900/4{,}000 \approx 10.7 \), rounded up to 11. At 35 W each, the room uses \( 11 \times 35 = 385 \) W, or 0.64 W/ft², which is below the roughly 1 W/ft² that energy codes commonly allow for classrooms, so the design meets the energy limit with margin.

Implementation: p5.js with updateCanvasSize() as the first statement in setup(), built-in createSlider and createSelect controls, and a simple uniform-illuminance calculation.

docs.title: Lighting Controls
docs.text: Lighting controls are the switches, dimmers, sensors, and software that turn lights on and off or adjust their output to match need. The simplest control is a manual switch. More capable controls include dimmers, which reduce light output and power, occupancy sensors that turn lights off when a room is empty, daylight sensors that dim electric light near windows, and time clocks or networked controls that follow a schedule. Energy codes commonly require automatic shutoff and daylight-responsive control in many commercial spaces, so controls are part of code compliance as well as convenience. The designer must also keep emergency lighting energized when normal power fails, and must therefore connect it ahead of the controls so that no switch or sensor can turn it off.

docs.title: Low-Voltage Systems
docs.text: Low-voltage systems are electrical systems that operate at 50 V or below, or at limited power, to carry signals and small amounts of power rather than to supply large loads. Their conductors are thin, their hazards are low, and their installation rules are different from those for power wiring. They include data and communications, fire alarm, security and access control, audio and video, and the control wiring of building automation. Low-voltage cables are generally kept separate from power conductors, to avoid electrical interference and to keep a fault in the power system from reaching the signal system. The electrical designer often designs the pathways, such as conduit and cable tray, and the power supplies, and then specialty consultants and contractors design and install the devices.

docs.title: Data and Communications
docs.text: Data and communications systems carry computer networks, telephones, and wireless signals through a building. The wiring is called structured cabling, with a standard layout in which twisted-pair copper cable (such as Category 6) runs from outlets in each room to a telecommunications room, where network equipment is mounted in racks. Copper links of this type are limited to about 328 feet (100 meters), so large buildings need several telecommunications rooms linked by fiber-optic cable. Many devices, including wireless access points and cameras, receive power over the same network cable, a technology called power over Ethernet (PoE). The designer must reserve rooms of adequate size with cooling and power, and conduit pathways. The size and location of the telecommunications room is among the decisions that must be made during schematic design.

docs.title: Fire Alarm Systems
docs.text:
A fire alarm system is an electrical system that detects a fire, warns the occupants, and signals other building systems and the fire department. It has three groups of parts. Initiating devices, such as smoke detectors, heat detectors, manual pull stations, and sprinkler flow switches (Chapter 14), sense the fire. The fire alarm control panel receives the signals and decides what to do. Notification appliances, such as horns, speakers, and strobe lights, alert the occupants, and the strobes serve people who cannot hear.

The panel also issues commands to other systems. It shuts down air handlers, closes smoke dampers, recalls elevators to the ground floor, and releases door locks on exit paths. Its power comes from the building, with a battery backup sized to run the system for hours and then sound the alarm. The system is supervised, meaning that the panel detects a cut wire or a dead battery and reports a trouble signal. Fire alarm design follows NFPA 72 and the building code, and the final system must be tested and accepted by the fire marshal (Chapter 18).

docs.title: Building Automation
docs.text: Building automation is a network of sensors, controllers, and software that monitors and controls the building's mechanical and electrical systems, so that they operate together according to schedules and setpoints. A thermostat is the simplest example. A building automation system extends the idea to hundreds of points. It can start the fans at six in the morning, lower the temperature setpoint on a night schedule, dim the lights when daylight is available, and send an alert when a pump fails. Devices from different manufacturers commonly share data through open communication standards such as BACnet. Automation saves energy and provides records, and it must be tested during commissioning (Chapter 2) to verify that every sequence works as the designers intended.

docs.title: Elevators
docs.text:
An elevator is a vertical transportation system, a car in a hoistway moved by an electric motor, that carries people and goods between floors. The two common types are traction elevators, where the car hangs from cables over a motor-driven sheave, and hydraulic elevators, where a pump pushes a piston. The electrical designer provides the power feeder, usually three-phase at 480 V, and a lockable disconnect switch near the equipment, and also provides lighting and receptacles in the machine room and the pit. A 25 horsepower motor draws on the order of 34 A at 460 V, a significant load in a mid-rise building.

Elevators must be coordinated with the fire alarm and the emergency power systems. On an alarm, the elevator is recalled to a designated floor and held there for firefighters, and a standby generator commonly powers at least one car during an outage. The equipment is also heavy and needs structural support in the hoistway and machine space. Riverbend is a one-story building and has no elevator, but any multi-story addition would introduce one.

docs.title: Photovoltaic Systems
docs.text:
A photovoltaic (PV) system is an electrical system that converts sunlight directly into electricity using solar panels. The main parts are the modules (panels), which produce direct current; the inverter, which converts it to alternating current at the building's voltage; the racking and wiring; and the disconnects and meters. Code requires a rapid shutdown feature that quickly de-energizes the conductors on the roof so that firefighters are not exposed to a live array. The system connects to the utility under an interconnection agreement, and the utility's rules determine how surplus power is credited.

Cold-climate details matter. Panels produce more voltage in cold weather, so the designer must make sure the inverter's maximum voltage is not exceeded on the coldest morning. Snow covers modules for part of the winter, and the roof must carry the weight of both the array and the snow (Chapter 6), and every roof penetration for the mounting hardware must be flashed (Chapter 13).

Worked example: a rooftop array for Riverbend. Assume an illustrative array of 75 modules of 400 W each, so the DC rating is \( 75 \times 400 = 30 \) kW. Each module covers about 21 ft², so the array occupies roughly \( 75 \times 21 = 1{,}575 \) ft², or about 18 percent of the 9,000 ft² roof. Upper Midwest sites commonly produce on the order of 1,200 to 1,400 kWh per kW of array per year, so taking 1,300 as an illustration gives \( 30 \times 1{,}300 = 39{,}000 \) kWh per year. The weight of modules and racking, on the order of 3 psf, is small compared with snow load, but the structural engineer must still approve it, especially over the 40 ft glulam span.

docs.title: Electric Vehicle Charging
docs.text:
Electric vehicle (EV) charging is the supply of electricity to the batteries of electric vehicles through electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE), the chargers and their wiring. Charging comes in three levels. Level 1 uses an ordinary 120 V outlet at about 1 to 2 kW. Level 2 uses a 208 or 240 V circuit at several kilowatts, typically 6 to 19 kW, and suits workplaces and homes. DC fast charging supplies direct current at tens or hundreds of kilowatts from a dedicated three-phase supply. Because charging runs for hours, the NEC treats an EV charger as a continuous load, so its circuit is sized at 125 percent of the charger's current. A charger delivering 32 A needs a 40 A circuit. Codes use the terms EV-capable (conduit and space for future chargers), EV-ready (a circuit installed to the location), and EV-installed (the charger itself).

Worked example: will four chargers fit? Suppose the owner of Riverbend wants four Level 2 chargers delivering 32 A each at 208 V. Each draws \( 32 \times 208 = 6{,}656 \) VA, so four draw 26,624 VA. Earlier, Riverbend's demand load was 59,250 VA, and a 200 A service at 208 V three-phase has a capacity of about 72,050 VA, leaving only about 12,800 VA of headroom. The four chargers do not fit at full power. The designer has three options: upgrade to a 400 A service, install fewer chargers, or use an energy management system that limits the chargers' combined output to the available headroom, which slows charging when the building is busy. A 36 kWh charging session at 6.66 kW takes about 5.4 hours, which suits a vehicle parked during an evening event.

You Can Follow the Electrical Design Through

You can now count a building's loads and turn them into a service size, read a one-line diagram and a set of electrical plans, explain why bonding trips a breaker, and describe how the electrical designer coordinates with the structural and mechanical engineers in every project phase. That is the working knowledge of the profession, and everything later in the book, from codes to energy, builds on it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The electrical designer plans the system, counts the loads, selects the equipment, and documents the result, with a licensed engineer responsible where the law requires. Electrical design phases parallel the project phases, and the earliest decisions about service, rooms, and space are the cheapest to make.
  • The structural engineer, mechanical engineer, and electrical designer compete for the same space and must coordinate. Gravity pipes, large ducts, and pressure pipes generally take priority over cable tray and conduit, and BIM clash detection finds conflicts before construction.
  • Service size is set by the demand load, not the connected load. A load calculation lists loads, converts them to VA, applies demand and continuous-load factors, sums them, and rounds up to the next standard size.
  • A one-line diagram shows the whole distribution system on one sheet, and the electrical plans, panel schedules, and specifications carry the details to the electrician.
  • Conductors are sized by ampacity and voltage drop. Conduit protects them and is limited by fill and bends. Bonding gives fault current a low-resistance path so the breaker trips, and grounding connects the system to the earth.
  • Lighting design uses lumens, footcandles, and efficacy, and the lumen method estimates the number of luminaires. Controls reduce energy use and are often required by the energy code.
  • Low-voltage systems, including data, fire alarm, and building automation, are kept separate from power wiring. Fire alarm systems detect, notify, and command other systems such as fans and elevators.
  • Photovoltaic systems and electric vehicle chargers are added loads and sources that affect the structure, the roof, and the service size, and they need early coordination with the utility and the other disciplines.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: How model codes and the Minnesota State Building Code are adopted, applied, and enforced through permits, plan review, and inspection. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 1, 2, 5, 9, 14, 15. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 20 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Building Codes 45 Model Codes 15 Building Official 10 International Building Code 10 Building Permits 4 Inspection and Testing 3 Minnesota State Building Code 3 Plan Review 3 Code Inspections 2 Code Enforcement 2 National Electrical Code 1 Residential Code 1 Fire Code 1 Plumbing Code 1 Mechanical Code 1 Accessibility Standards 1 Zoning 1 Certificate of Occupancy 1 Variances and Appeals 1 Referenced Standards 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
  • Chapter 2: The Design and Construction Process
  • Chapter 5: Properties of Building Materials
  • Chapter 9: Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater
  • Chapter 14: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
  • Chapter 15: Electrical Fundamentals and Building Service

The Rulebook Every Building Plays By

Every wall, stair, outlet, and exit sign you will ever specify has to pass through a set of rules written by people who studied what went wrong in past buildings. Learn how those rules are organized and who enforces them, and you will stop fearing the permit counter and start planning for it. Let's build it right!

The earlier chapters explained how buildings carry loads, manage heat and moisture, and distribute power. This chapter explains the legal framework that decides whether a particular building may be built and occupied. A building can be well designed and still be refused a permit, or can be built carefully and still be refused permission to open. Codes, permits, and inspections are how a community checks that its buildings meet a shared minimum before people use them.

We return to the Riverbend Youth Center from Chapter 2, the invented one-story, wood-framed community building in Minneapolis with a 40 ft multipurpose room, three classrooms, a kitchen, and offices. Every number attached to Riverbend here is illustrative. Code values change with each edition and each jurisdiction, so where this chapter mentions a specific value it is hedged, and your job in practice is always to read the edition in force for your project.

docs.title: Building Codes
docs.text:
Building codes are legally enforceable sets of minimum requirements for the design, construction, alteration, and use of buildings, adopted by a government to protect public health, safety, and general welfare. The authority comes from the police power, the long-standing ability of a state to regulate private activity when public safety is at stake. A code is therefore not advice or a best-practice guide. It is law, and a building that violates it can be denied a permit, stopped during construction, or refused an occupancy approval.

Codes grew out of disasters. Many provisions that now look routine, such as limits on how close buildings may stand, requirements for more than one exit, and sprinklers in certain buildings, were added after fires, collapses, and building-related illnesses showed what unregulated construction costs. Reading a code with this history in mind makes it easier to remember, because each requirement answers a specific failure. The code is also a minimum. It sets the least performance the community will accept, and it says nothing about whether a building is comfortable, efficient, or beautiful.

docs.title: How a Code Is Organized
docs.text:
Building codes are organized so that a designer can start from the building's use and follow a chain of questions to the requirements that apply. Most codes begin with administrative provisions that say who enforces the code, when a permit is needed, and how appeals work. A definitions section follows. The technical provisions then address use and occupancy, fire protection, means of egress, accessibility, the building envelope, structural design, and the materials chapters for wood, steel, concrete, and masonry. The last part lists the referenced standards, covered later in this chapter.

Requirements come in two styles. A prescriptive requirement states exactly what to do, such as a minimum thickness or a required component, and it is easy to check. A performance requirement states the result that must be achieved, such as resisting fire for a stated time, and leaves the means to the designer, who must then show by test or analysis that the result is met. Most codes mix both. Prescriptive paths are faster for ordinary buildings, and performance paths give room for unusual designs.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Code as a Procedure
docs.text:
Code use is a procedure: classify the building, find the controlling provision, calculate, and then check. Consider how the design team applies it to the Riverbend multipurpose room, which measures 2,400 ft² of usable floor area. The team first decides what the room is used for, which determines its occupancy classification, a concept Chapter 18 develops. A room with tables and chairs for meals and gatherings is an assembly use. The code then assigns a floor area per occupant, a number of square feet allowed for each person, and the occupant load (the number of people the space must be designed to hold) follows by division:

\[ \text{occupant load} = \frac{\text{floor area}}{\text{floor area per occupant}} \]

For assembly space with tables and chairs, the code commonly uses about 15 net ft² per person, which gives \( 2{,}400 / 15 = 160 \) people. If the room will often be set up with chairs in tight rows, the code treats it as concentrated use, commonly about 7 net ft² per person, and the load becomes \( 2{,}400 / 7 \approx 343 \), or roughly 340 people. The designer then looks up how many exits a space of that load needs. Codes commonly require at least two exits once the load passes a small threshold, and more exits as the load rises. In practice the team verifies every factor against the adopted edition, since the values here are illustrative.

The point is not the answer but the chain: use, factor, load, exits. Each later step uses the result of the one before, which is why classifying the occupancy correctly at the start matters so much.

The Code Is a Floor, Not a Ceiling

Think of the code as the floor of a room: you may not go below it, but nothing stops you from building higher. A design that meets the code only just barely may still leave the owner with a building that is drafty, noisy, or expensive to run.

Three terms need a short definition before we look at the diagram below. A model code is a code written by a private standards organization instead of a legislature, so it has no legal force until a government adopts it. To adopt a code means that a legislature or agency enacts it by law, usually with changes called amendments that suit local conditions. The authority having jurisdiction is the government office that enforces the code for a particular project. Later sections treat each in turn.

A side strip shows the question each layer answers. The canvas fills the container width, has a height of 480 px, and redraws on window resize.

Interactions: Hovering over a layer shows a tooltip with a one-sentence definition. Clicking a layer opens an infobox with three items: who writes it, who enforces it, and a Riverbend example, such as the edition in force on the date of the permit application. A toggle labeled "Amendment on" adds a highlighted Minnesota amendment to the state layer and shows how the project-level requirement changes. A button labeled "Which rule wins?" presents a short conflict, such as a local ordinance that is stricter than the state code, and asks the student to choose the controlling layer. The answer is checked immediately with a plain-language explanation.

Beau's Tip: Find the Edition Before You Calculate

Before you pull a single number from any code, write down the edition and the Minnesota amendments in force on your permit date at the top of your calculation sheet. A number from the wrong edition is the quietest way to fail a plan review.

docs.title: Model Codes
docs.text:
Model codes are comprehensive codes developed by private organizations through consensus processes so that governments do not each have to write their own. Committees of building officials, engineers, architects, manufacturers, and fire service members propose and debate changes, and the organization publishes a new edition on a regular cycle, typically every three years. Because the document is written for national use, it is general and does not reflect any one state's climate or law.

The advantage is consistency. A contractor who knows the model code in one state can use it in the next, manufacturers can test and label products to one set of requirements, and a state can adopt a document that has already been through years of review. The cost is a lag. A state takes time to review each new edition, hold hearings, add amendments, and write the rules, so the edition in force for a project is often one or two cycles behind the newest published edition.

Worked example: which edition governs Riverbend? Suppose, illustratively, that a model code organization publishes a new edition in 2024, while Minnesota's adopted rules still reference the edition published in 2021. The Riverbend team applies for its permit in 2025. The permit is reviewed against the edition in force in Minnesota on the application date, so the 2021 edition, plus Minnesota's amendments, governs. A designer who used the new 2024 edition for the stair dimensions would find that the reviewer measures the design against different numbers. Amendments illustrate why a model code is never used alone. Minnesota, for example, commonly amends model provisions to reflect its cold climate, such as the depth of footings needed to get below frost, a topic covered in Chapter 10. The only safe practice is to confirm the adopted edition and the amendments with the building official at the start of design.

docs.title: International Building Code
docs.text:
The International Building Code (IBC) is the model code for most buildings other than one- and two-family houses and townhouses. The International Code Council (ICC) publishes it and it is the basis for the commercial building code in Minnesota and in most other states. It covers structure, fire protection, egress, accessibility, the envelope, and the materials used to build, so for a building like Riverbend it is the central document, with several others working alongside it.

The IBC follows the organization described earlier, and the sequence of its technical chapters matches the order in which a designer works. Chapter numbers shift slightly between editions, so this list names groups of provisions rather than numbers.

  1. Scope, administration, and definitions.
  2. Use and occupancy classification, which sorts buildings by what people do in them.
  3. Height, area, and construction types, which limit how big a building may be and what it is made of.
  4. Fire and smoke protection, including fire-resistance ratings and fire protection systems.
  5. Means of egress, the path people follow to leave a building, and accessibility.
  6. Interior environment and energy provisions, including light, ventilation, and references to the energy code.
  7. Exterior walls and roofs.
  8. Structural design, soils, foundations, and the material chapters for concrete, masonry, steel, and wood.
  9. Special inspections and tests, and a closing list of referenced standards.

Worked example: routing five Riverbend questions. The first column below lists questions the team asks at different points in design. The second names the group of IBC provisions where the answer starts.

Riverbend question Where the answer starts Is the multipurpose room an assembly use? Use and occupancy classification How large may the wood-framed building be without sprinklers? Height, area, and construction types How long must the glued-laminated beams resist fire, if at all? Fire-resistance provisions, tied to construction type How many exits does the classroom wing need? Means of egress What snow load must the roof carry? Structural design, which refers to a loads standard

The Code Book Looks Bigger Than It Is

A model code can run to hundreds of pages, and the many exceptions make everyone feel lost at first. You already know how to follow a chain of dependent steps from Chapter 2, so start at occupancy classification and follow the cross-references one at a time, writing each answer down as you go.

The chain in the table is the reason most designers use a code-routing habit: ask the question, find the group, and follow the cross-references until the requirement is fully resolved. The following MicroSim lets you practice that habit.

docs.title: Minnesota State Building Code
docs.text:
The Minnesota State Building Code is the set of building regulations that Minnesota adopts into state rules and applies to construction across the state. The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry administers the adoption process, and it generally adopts a model code such as the IBC with Minnesota amendments. The state publishes the result as a set of codes by subject, for example the commercial building code, the residential code, the energy codes, and the accessibility rules.

The code applies statewide, and most cities and many counties administer it through their own building officials, who issue permits and perform inspections. Local government may add some rules of its own, such as zoning, but generally cannot weaken the state code. Because of this layered structure, the first practical question on a Minneapolis project is who the authority having jurisdiction is and which edition they enforce. The answer is on the city's permitting website or from a call to the building department.

docs.title: The Family of Technical Codes
docs.text: A building is regulated by several subject-specific codes in addition to the building code, because each building system has its own specialists and hazards. The sections below define each, and the table that follows summarizes who publishes and who typically enforces each one.

docs.title: National Electrical Code
docs.text: The National Electrical Code (NEC) is the standard for the safe installation of electrical wiring and equipment, published as NFPA 70 by the National Fire Protection Association and revised on a three-year cycle. It governs conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding, and the equipment introduced in Chapters 15 and 16. It is an installation code and not a design manual, so it sets safety limits and leaves the choice of design to the engineer. States adopt it into law. In Minnesota, the state's electrical program, rather than the city building inspector, typically handles electrical inspection, which is one reason an electrical designer pulls a separate electrical permit.

docs.title: Residential Code
docs.text: The residential code, in model form the International Residential Code (IRC), covers one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses up to a stated height. It is a single prescriptive document that includes structural, mechanical, plumbing, and energy provisions, so a builder can find nearly everything in one place. Buildings outside its scope, such as apartment buildings and commercial buildings like Riverbend, fall under the IBC.

docs.title: Fire Code
docs.text: The fire code governs the use and maintenance of buildings after they are built, whereas the building code governs how they are built. It covers matters such as keeping exits unobstructed, storing hazardous materials, testing sprinklers and alarms, and limiting crowds in assembly spaces. Fire marshals and fire departments typically enforce it, and Chapter 18 treats fire protection and life-safety requirements in detail.

docs.title: Plumbing Code and Mechanical Code
docs.text: The plumbing code regulates water supply, drainage, venting, fixtures, and backflow prevention in the systems described in Chapter 14. The mechanical code regulates heating, ventilation, air conditioning, exhaust, fuel-burning equipment, and ductwork. Each sets installation requirements that protect health, such as safe drinking water and safe combustion venting, and each is typically enforced by its own inspectors. States vary in which model plumbing code they build on, so confirm the Minnesota version for the project.

docs.title: Accessibility Standards
docs.text: Accessibility standards require that buildings be usable by people with disabilities, including people who use wheelchairs, have limited vision, or have limited hearing. They cover accessible routes, ramps, door clearances, restrooms, parking, and signage. Two sources apply. The building code references a technical standard on accessible design, and a federal civil rights law, the Americans with Disabilities Act, separately requires accessibility for public accommodations and public buildings. A design may pass the building code and still need a check against the federal requirements, so the designer reviews both.

docs.title: Referenced Standards
docs.text:
Referenced standards are documents written by standards organizations that a code names and thereby makes enforceable. A building code cannot repeat every detail of every test method and design procedure, so it cites the document instead. The cited edition becomes part of the code to the extent the code references it, which is why the code carries a list of referenced standards.

Worked example: tracing the Riverbend beams. The IBC requires the glued-laminated beams to carry the design loads. The IBC points to a loads standard, ASCE/SEI 7, for snow, wind, and live loads, and to the wood design specification from the American Wood Council for the strength of the wood members. The beams must also be made by a producer who meets an industry manufacturing standard. A single sentence in the building code therefore opens a trail through three or more documents. A designer who reads only the building code and never opens the referenced standards has read part of the requirement.

The table below summarizes the family of codes that this section defined.

Code Typical publisher Covers Riverbend example International Building Code ICC Structure, fire, egress, envelope Beam size, exits, fire ratings National Electrical Code NFPA Electrical installation Switchboard, grounding Plumbing code ICC or IAPMO (varies) Water, drainage, venting Kitchen waste, restroom fixtures Mechanical code ICC HVAC, exhaust, ducts Rooftop unit, kitchen hood Fire code ICC Use and maintenance for fire safety Exit signs, extinguishers Accessibility standards ICC and federal Accessible routes and fixtures Ramp, restrooms

docs.title: Zoning
docs.text:
Zoning is a local land-use law that controls what may be built on a parcel and how the building sits on it. A city divides its land into districts, and each district limits the permitted uses, the building height, the lot coverage, the setbacks (the required distances between building and property lines), the amount of parking, and sometimes the appearance. Zoning answers the question "may we build this here?", while the building code answers "is this built safely?"

Both reviews are needed, and zoning usually comes first, because a building that is not permitted on the site never reaches building-code review. A zoning rule can also shape the structure: a setback that pushes a building toward a property line can trigger fire-resistance requirements for the wall closest to it. For Riverbend, the team confirms before schematic design that a community center is a permitted use in the site's district and that the footprint respects the setbacks.

docs.title: Building Official
docs.text:
The building official is the person designated by a jurisdiction to administer and enforce the building code. The title may be building official, code official, or building inspector, and in larger cities the office employs plan reviewers and inspectors under that person's direction. The official's authority comes from the code and local law. It includes the power to issue permits, to review plans, to inspect work, to accept alternative materials and methods that meet the code's intent, to order unsafe work stopped, and to deny the occupancy certificate.

The role has a limit that students sometimes miss. The building official checks that the work complies with the code and does not design the building, manage the project, or guarantee quality. The official also cannot waive the code on request. A request to depart from it must go through a formal process, discussed under variances and appeals. Treating the official as a partner in problem-solving, not an adversary, usually produces the best outcomes.

Worked example: a pre-application meeting. Before finishing design development, the Riverbend architect meets the building official to confirm three items. The first is the edition and amendments in force, and the second is whether the kitchen's cooking equipment will be treated as an assembly accessory use. The third is the preferred way to submit drawings. The official answers the first and third directly and asks for a written narrative on the second. The 45-minute meeting costs almost nothing and removes three sources of later conflict. Without it, any of those items could have surfaced during plan review, after the construction documents were complete, when a change would be expensive.

docs.title: Building Permits
docs.text:
A building permit is the official written authorization from the jurisdiction to begin specified construction work. It is issued after the jurisdiction reviews the plans, and it records that the work will be inspected. Typically a permit is required for new buildings, additions, alterations that change structure or systems, and the installation of major mechanical, plumbing, and electrical equipment. Cosmetic work such as painting generally does not require one. Permits also protect the owner, since later buyers, lenders, and insurers often ask for the permit and inspection records.

Applying means submitting an application form, construction documents, and the fee, and in many cities the fee is calculated from the estimated construction value. The permit card or posted placard stays on site, and the permit expires if work does not begin or stops for a long period. Working without a permit is a violation that can bring stop-work orders, fines, and the cost of opening finished walls so that inspectors can see the work.

Worked example: permit timeline for Riverbend. The team uses an illustrative review schedule to check whether the permit fits the construction start date. The jurisdiction takes 15 business days for the first plan review. The design team needs 5 business days to answer comments and resubmit, and the second review takes 10 business days.

\[ 15 + 5 + 10 = 30 \text{ business days} \]

Thirty business days is six working weeks. If the owner wants to break ground on a Monday in early April, the application must be submitted at least six weeks earlier, and more if the review comes back with additional comments. A contractor may also hold a separate, earlier permit for site grading, so that excavation can begin while review of the building proper continues. The key lesson is that the permit is a schedule activity, which belongs on the critical path of Chapter 2.

Watch Out: Work Without a Permit

A common trap is starting a small piece of work because it seems too minor to need a permit. The danger is that unpermitted work can force you to open finished walls later, so call the building department first and ask whether the work needs one.

docs.title: Plan Review
docs.text:
Plan review is the process by which the building official examines the construction documents for compliance with the code before issuing a permit. Reviewers check the drawings against occupancy classification, construction type, area limits, fire-resistance ratings, egress, accessibility, structural design, energy, and the mechanical, plumbing, and electrical systems. For some buildings, other agencies, such as the fire marshal or a state office, also review plans. The reviewer returns a list of comments or corrections, and the design team revises the documents and responds in writing.

Reviewers can only judge what the documents show. Clear code summaries on the drawings, with occupancy, construction type, areas, occupant loads, and egress widths all stated, shorten review because the reviewer can see how the designer applied the code. Plans approved by the jurisdiction are stamped and kept on site, and the inspectors use them as the standard for the work.

docs.title: Code Inspections
docs.text:
Code inspections are visits by the building official's inspectors to the site, during construction, to verify that the work matches the approved plans and the code. They happen at defined points, typically before the work is covered and cannot be seen. The contractor requests each inspection, the inspector examines the work, and the result is recorded as approved or as a list of corrections. A failed item is fixed and reinspected before work proceeds.

A typical sequence for a wood-framed building includes the following inspections.

  • Footing and foundation, before concrete is placed.
  • Underground plumbing and electrical, before backfill or slab.
  • Framing, once the structure and rough-in are visible.
  • Insulation and air sealing, before drywall hides them.
  • Final, when everything is complete.

The inspector sees only a sample of the work on a given day, and inspection does not replace the contractor's own quality control.

docs.title: Inspection and Testing
docs.text:
Inspection and testing is the broader category of checks that includes the official's inspections plus tests that show whether materials and systems perform. Some tests are required on materials, such as strength tests on concrete cylinders, compaction tests on soil under footings, and welding inspection on structural steel. Others are required on systems, such as pressure tests of piping, acceptance tests of fire alarms, and airtightness tests of the enclosure, the subject of Chapters 11 and 12.

For structural and other critical work, the code often requires special inspections: inspections performed by an independent qualified agency hired by the owner, not by the building department. The building official reviews their reports. Testing agencies provide the data the inspector cannot gather by looking, and the reports become part of the project record that supports the certificate of occupancy.

Watch Out: Covering Work Before It Is Inspected

It is tempting to pour or close up a wall when the inspector is running late. The risk is that the inspector may order the work uncovered, which costs far more than waiting, so confirm every required inspection is signed off before concealing the work.

Clicking a box opens an infobox with a two-sentence definition drawn from this chapter. A toggle on each diamond lets the student force a failure and see the loop. docs.title: Code Enforcement
docs.text:
Code enforcement is the set of actions a jurisdiction uses to compel compliance with the code. During construction, enforcement means refusing to issue a permit until the plans comply, issuing a correction notice for defects found at inspection, and issuing a stop-work order when work proceeds unsafely or without a permit. For existing buildings, enforcement continues through complaints and periodic inspections, with notices of violation, fines, and in the most serious cases orders to vacate or demolish an unsafe building.

Enforcement works by consequence. A building that has not passed final inspection cannot legally be occupied, a contractor who repeatedly fails inspections may face penalties, and an owner who ignores a notice may be fined or taken to court. Most enforcement is routine and cooperative: the inspector identifies a problem, the contractor corrects it, and the process continues. The legal tools exist for the cases where cooperation fails.

docs.title: Certificate of Occupancy
docs.text:
A certificate of occupancy is the document issued by the building official that states a building has been inspected and complies with the code, and that it may be occupied for its stated use. It lists the occupancy classification and may state the approved occupant load, which is the figure for which the building was designed. Chapter 2 introduced it as the last step of closeout. It requires final approval from the building official, and often from the fire marshal and other reviewers, and it usually depends on the test reports and corrections described above.

Some jurisdictions issue a temporary certificate of occupancy, which permits use of part of the building, or the whole of it, while minor items remain unfinished. If an owner changes the use of a building later, for example from offices to a restaurant, a new certificate is commonly required, since the new use brings new code requirements.

docs.title: Variances and Appeals
docs.text:
A variance is a formal permission to depart from a requirement when strict compliance would cause unusual hardship, and an appeal is a request that a higher authority review a decision by the building official. The two are related but distinct. The usual path starts with a conversation, then a written request to the building official to accept an alternative that meets the intent of the code, and finally a hearing before a board of appeals if the designer disagrees with the official's ruling. In Minnesota, the appeal route can continue to the state level.

Zoning variances follow a different path, since they go to a local board that decides on departures from setbacks, height limits, or use restrictions. A variance is a poor way to rescue a design that ignored the code. It works best when the designer shows that the alternative achieves the same level of safety as the prescribed rule, with evidence such as an engineering analysis or a test.

You Can Navigate the Rulebook

You can now explain how a model code like the IBC becomes the Minnesota State Building Code, trace a requirement through occupancy, occupant load, and exits, and follow a project from zoning check and permit through plan review, inspection, and certificate of occupancy. That is the whole path from a drawing to a legally occupied building.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Building codes are enforceable minimums adopted under the police power to protect public health, safety, and welfare. They set a floor, not a target for good design.
  • Codes use prescriptive and performance requirements, and designers apply them as a procedure: classify the occupancy, find the controlling provision, calculate, and check.
  • Model codes such as the International Building Code are written by private organizations and have no legal force until a state or local government adopts them, usually with amendments.
  • The Minnesota State Building Code applies statewide and is typically administered locally, so confirm the edition in force and the authority having jurisdiction at the start of design.
  • Subject codes, including the National Electrical Code, residential, fire, plumbing, and mechanical codes, and accessibility standards, work alongside the building code, and referenced standards extend each one.
  • Zoning decides whether a use is allowed on a site, while the building code decides whether the building is safe.
  • The building official administers the code but does not design the building or waive requirements; permits, plan review, inspections, and testing are the checks, and the certificate of occupancy is the final approval.
  • Enforcement tools include correction notices and stop-work orders, and variances and appeals provide a formal way to propose alternatives that meet the code's intent.

docs.title: Fire Protection and Life Safety Requirements
Summary
docs.text: The code requirements for occupancy, construction type, fire-resistance ratings, egress, and emergency power that protect occupants. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 1, 5, 14, 15, 16, 17. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 11 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Occupancy Classification 6 Life Safety 6 Fire-Resistance Ratings 4 Emergency Power 3 Construction Types 2 Means of Egress 2 Generators 1 Uninterruptible Power Supply 1 Fire Separations 1 Travel Distance 1 Allowable Building Area 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
  • Chapter 5: Properties of Building Materials
  • Chapter 14: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
  • Chapter 15: Electrical Fundamentals and Building Service
  • Chapter 16: Electrical Distribution, Lighting, and Design Team Coordination
  • Chapter 17: Building Codes, Permits, and Enforcement

Buying Time to Get Out

The best thing a building can do in a fire is give everyone inside enough time to walk out. By the end of this chapter you will know the handful of code ideas that buy that time, and you will be able to look at a floor plan and say how it does it. Let's build it right!

Chapter 17 explained that the building code is a chain of questions that starts with what the building is used for. This chapter follows that chain through the part of the code that protects human life from fire. The requirements can look like a pile of unrelated numbers: a rating of one hour here, a distance of a few hundred feet there. They are in fact a single strategy with several layers, and once you see the strategy, the numbers have a purpose.

We again use the invented Riverbend Youth Center from Chapter 2, a one-story, wood-framed Minneapolis building of about 9,000 ft² with a 40 ft multipurpose room, three 600 ft² classrooms, a kitchen, and offices. All Riverbend numbers are illustrative, and every code value in this chapter is hedged, because the adopted edition and the building official control what applies to a real project.

docs.title: Life Safety
docs.text:
Life safety is the design objective of protecting people in a building from fire, smoke, and other emergencies long enough for them to escape or be rescued. It differs from property protection, which aims to save the building and its contents. A building can be a total loss and still have a successful life-safety outcome, because every occupant got out. The code concentrates on life safety first, which explains why many of its rules concern escape routes and smoke, not the building's survival.

The hazard is not only flame. Burning produces hot gases and smoke that can fill a room long before flames reach the people in it, and smoke is a leading cause of fire deaths. Life safety therefore depends on detecting the fire quickly, limiting its growth and spread, and getting people out before conditions become unsurvivable. No single measure does all of that, so the code uses layered protection, listed below.

  1. Prevent ignition. Control fuel sources, electrical faults, and ignition hazards, such as the kitchen cooking equipment.
  2. Detect and alert. Smoke detectors and alarms warn occupants early; Chapter 14 introduced the fire protection systems.
  3. Control and suppress. Sprinklers, also introduced in Chapter 14, limit the fire's size.
  4. Compartment. Fire-resistance-rated walls and floors keep fire and smoke in one area.
  5. Escape. Exits that are sufficient, close, and clear let people leave.
  6. Keep the escape route usable. Emergency lighting and signs stay on if the power fails.

Worked example: the race between smoke and people. Fire engineers frame the goal as a race between two times. The available safe egress time (ASET) is how long it takes for smoke and heat to make the escape route unsurvivable. The required safe egress time (RSET) is how long occupants need to get out, which is the sum of the time to detect and alarm, the time people take to recognize the alarm and start moving, and the time to walk out. Suppose that, in the Riverbend multipurpose room, a fire starts in the kitchen. The alarm sounds 1.0 minute after ignition, occupants take 1.5 minutes to respond and gather themselves, and walking out takes 1.0 minute, so RSET is \( 1.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 3.5 \) minutes. A smoke analysis finds that the room becomes untenable at 6 minutes. The safety margin is \( 6.0 - 3.5 = 2.5 \) minutes. If one of two exits is blocked, walking time doubles to 2.0 minutes, RSET becomes 4.5 minutes, and the margin falls to 1.5 minutes. The code's requirements for exits, alarms, and sprinklers are each ways to lengthen ASET or shorten RSET. The times here are illustrative.

No Single Layer Saves the Day

Think of the layers as slices of Swiss cheese: each one has holes, but the holes seldom line up. That is why a building with sprinklers still needs exits, and why a building with rated walls still needs alarms.

A vertical marker shows the available safe egress time, and the gap between the two ends is labeled with the margin in minutes, shown in green when positive and red when negative. A small floor plan of the Riverbend multipurpose room with two exits sits below the timeline. The canvas fills the container width, has a height of 480 px, and redraws on window resize.

docs.title: Occupancy Classification
docs.text:
Occupancy classification is the code's way of sorting a building, or a part of a building, by how it is used and therefore by how much fire risk it carries. Chapter 1 observed that the building type controls which code provisions apply, and this is the mechanism. The classification is the first question in the code-reading chain from Chapter 17, since the occupant load factors, the number of exits, the sprinkler requirements, and the allowed building area all depend on it.

The International Building Code groups uses into ten letter-coded categories, named for what people do in the space: gathering is Assembly (A), working in an office is Business (B), and learning in a school is Educational (E). The following table summarizes the principal groups.

Group Use Everyday examples A Assembly Theaters, restaurants, churches, community halls B Business Offices, banks, clinics for outpatient care E Educational Schools through twelfth grade F Factory Manufacturing H High hazard Facilities with large amounts of explosive or toxic materials I Institutional Hospitals, jails, care facilities with people who cannot easily leave M Mercantile Stores R Residential Apartments, hotels, dormitories S Storage Warehouses U Utility Sheds, barns, garages

Each group has subdivisions, such as A-3 for assembly uses that include community halls. Risk depends on who is in the building and how they behave: schoolchildren need adult direction, a theater audience is dense and unfamiliar with the exits, and hospital patients may be unable to move. Higher-risk groups face stricter rules.

Many buildings have more than one use. A smaller use that supports the main one, such as an office inside a school, is an accessory occupancy, and the code commonly allows it to be treated as part of the main use if it occupies no more than about 10 percent of the floor area of its story. Larger secondary uses create a mixed occupancy, which must either be separated by fire-rated construction or be designed to meet the strictest requirement that applies anywhere in the building.

Worked example: classifying Riverbend. The table below compares each Riverbend space, taken from the Chapter 2 program, with a gross story area of 9,000 ft².

Space Area (ft²) Share of 9,000 ft² Likely classification Multipurpose room 2,400 26.7% Assembly (A-3) Classrooms 1,800 20.0% Educational or assembly, depending on the program Kitchen 500 5.6% Accessory to assembly Offices 360 4.0% Business, accessory Lobby and restrooms 900 10.0% Part of the main use

The kitchen and offices fall below the commonly used 10 percent threshold, so they can be treated as accessory. The classrooms, at 20 percent, do not, so Riverbend is a mixed occupancy. The classification of the classrooms depends on the age of the students and how many hours the programs run, since the code defines educational use by those thresholds. The team documents its reasoning, then confirms the conclusion with the building official in the pre-application meeting that Chapter 17 described, because a classification error cascades through every later calculation.

Beau's Tip: Tabulate Every Room First

Before you declare a building a single occupancy, list every room with its area and its use, then calculate each room's share of the story. The percentages show immediately whether you have accessory uses or a mixed occupancy.

docs.title: Construction Types
docs.text:
Construction types are the code's five categories for classifying a building by the materials of its structure and the fire resistance of its parts. The categories are Type I through Type V. Types I and II use noncombustible materials such as steel and concrete, Type III combines noncombustible exterior walls with combustible interior framing, Type IV is heavy timber, and Type V is ordinary combustible construction, usually wood framing. Types I, II, III, and V are further divided into subtypes labeled A and B, where A indicates protected construction (structural elements have fire-resistance ratings) and B indicates unprotected construction (fewer or no ratings required). The table restates these categories.

Type Main structure Idea in plain terms I Noncombustible, heavily protected Concrete or steel frames with high ratings II Noncombustible Steel or concrete, with less protection III Noncombustible exterior walls, combustible interior framing Masonry walls with wood floors and roof IV Heavy timber (and mass timber in newer editions) Large timber members that resist fire by charring V Combustible, usually wood-frame Ordinary wood-frame buildings

Noncombustible does not mean fireproof, since unprotected steel loses much of its strength at the temperatures of a developed fire. The type matters because it sets the fire-resistance rating each part of the structure must have, and with the occupancy it limits the building's height and area. Riverbend, a one-story wood-framed building with glued-laminated beams, is a candidate for several types depending on how the team protects the members, so the designers choose the type deliberately as a trade-off between structure cost and allowable size.

docs.title: Allowable Building Area
docs.text:
Allowable building area is the largest floor area the code permits on a single floor of a building, determined by the combination of occupancy group and construction type. The code lists a tabulated area for each pairing. Combustible, unprotected construction of a high-risk occupancy gets a small tabulated area, and noncombustible, protected construction of a lower-risk occupancy gets a much larger one. The idea is that a bigger fire compartment holds more fuel and more people, so it needs better construction.

Two common adjustments raise the tabulated area. A building protected by an automatic sprinkler system may receive an increase, since sprinklers limit fire size. A building with a large share of its perimeter facing open space, called frontage, may receive another increase, because firefighters can reach it from several sides and fire is less likely to jump to a neighboring structure. An area that is too small for the program can be solved by changing the construction type, by adding sprinklers, or by dividing the building with a fire wall, a wall so robust that the code treats the two sides as separate buildings. The team compares the programmed area from Chapter 2 with the tabulated area early, since an area problem found during construction documents can force a change in construction type.

docs.title: Fire-Resistance Ratings
docs.text:
A fire-resistance rating is the length of time, in hours, that a building assembly such as a wall, floor, beam, or column can withstand a standard fire test while performing its function. The standard test, ASTM E119, exposes the assembly to a prescribed rise in furnace temperature. To earn a rating, the assembly must keep carrying its load if it is structural, must not let flame or hot gases pass through, and must not let the temperature on the unexposed side rise too far. Common ratings are 1 hour and 2 hours. The rating does not predict how long a real building will last in a real fire. It is a standardized measure that lets designers compare assemblies.

Ratings belong to assemblies, not to materials. A gypsum board by itself has no rating, but a stud wall with specified framing, insulation, and layers of gypsum board on each side, tested as a unit, does. Designers find ratings in the code's tables of prescribed assemblies, in listings from testing laboratories, and in calculation methods the code accepts for certain materials, notably heavy timber and concrete. Chapter 5 described how materials behave in fire. Ratings turn that behavior into a number a code can use.

Worked example: a glued-laminated beam in a fire. Wood chars when it burns, and the char layer insulates the wood beneath it, so a large timber member loses strength by losing section rather than by softening. Designers estimate the loss with a charring rate, which for this example is a nominal 1.5 in per hour on each exposed face. Consider a Riverbend beam 8.75 in wide and 24 in deep, exposed on its bottom and two sides. Its resistance to bending depends on its section modulus, \( S = bd^2/6 \), where \( b \) is the width and \( d \) is the depth. Before the fire:

\[ S = \frac{8.75 \times 24^2}{6} = 840 \text{ in}^3 \]

After one hour, 1.5 in of each exposed face has charred, so the remaining section is 5.75 in wide (8.75 minus two sides) and 22.5 in deep (24 minus the bottom):

\[ S = \frac{5.75 \times 22.5^2}{6} \approx 485 \text{ in}^3 \]

That is about 58 percent of the original capacity. For the beam to survive one hour, the designer must show that the remaining section can still carry the design loads, which are lower in a fire than in normal service. If it cannot, a deeper or wider beam is used. The method is a simplified illustration, and the code and a structural engineer specify the actual design procedure and char values.

A dark char layer grows inward on the exposed faces as the exposure time increases, and the remaining section is drawn in tan.
